speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DIRECTIVE OF CABINET COUNCIL AUTHORIZING EXEMPTION FROM PROVISIONS OF SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
The government cannot consent to this motion, for many reasons. One results from the express terms of the oath of office of the members of the privy council. It reads in part as follows:
You do solemnly promise and swear that you will serve His Majesty truly and faithfully in the place of his council in this His Majesty's Dominion of Canada; you will keep close and secret all such matters as shall be treated, debated and resolved on in privy council, without publishing or disclosing the same or any part thereof, by word, writing, or any otherwise to any person out of the same council, but to such only as be of the council . . .
That is a part of the oath of office. Now, this motion calls for a copy of a directive of the cabinet council of March or April, 1950. The Minister of Transport stated in debate the other night that there had been an oral directive. Whether or not it is proper to call it a directive is a matter which might be discussed. What happens is that when a minister of the crown has, by statute, the power to do a certain thing, and it is a mere matter of routine he does not necessarily discuss it with his colleagues. But because his conduct involves the responsibility of all the members of the government, if it is a matter about which he is in any doubt or about which he feels there may be some embarrassment, it is usual for him to discuss it with his colleagues before making his decision. The result of that discussion may be called a directive, or it may be called an opinion. It is an expression of the views of his colleagues upon the manner in which he might exercise the powers that

Motions for Papers
are given to him by statute. Prior to 1940 no -memoranda were kept of such discussions or *decisions in council. During the war, in 1940, it became the practice to keep memoranda of the discussions in the war committee of the cabinet; and in 1944 or 1945 the practice was started of keeping memoranda of these discussions which took place in cabinet. But these memoranda cannot be published.
When this question was raised I suggested that I might get permission from the administrator not to table them-they certainly *could not be published in that way-but to show them confidentially to the leader of the opposition. On consideration, however, it was found that such a procedure would establish a precedent which might some day embarrass whomsoever occupies the office I now occupy, and that it would not be proper to establish precedents which would in any way depart from this constitutional tradition that the matters treated, debated and resolved on in privy council cannot be published to any who are not of the privy council.
Although I do not wish to establish any precedent that would impinge upon that traditional constitutional rule, I think that such information as can be given in confidence to any member of parliament who is desirous of obtaining it, .and can be given without violating the express terms of the privy councillor's oath, can be expected to be given-. But from the time of confederation up to 1944 there were no memoranda of what took place in these deliberations, and nothing in writing resulted except the recommendations that were put before the governor general and that received his assent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DIRECTIVE OF CABINET COUNCIL AUTHORIZING EXEMPTION FROM PROVISIONS OF SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: DIRECTIVE OF CABINET COUNCIL AUTHORIZING EXEMPTION FROM PROVISIONS OF SHIPPING ACT
speechtext: Before the leader of the opposition speaks, may I remind the house that, under standing order 51, these notices of motion for the production of papers are to be put forthwith without debate. I hope there will be no misunderstanding of the rules. I -cannot allow debate. On the other hand, I think I should allow the leader of the opposition to make some reply to what has been said-.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DIRECTIVE OF CABINET COUNCIL AUTHORIZING EXEMPTION FROM PROVISIONS OF SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was because the Prime Minister had carefully explained the reasons that I felt it was appropriate that some comment should be made, because these records establish a precedent in regard to matters of this kind. The Prime Minister has referred to a well-established and reasonable tradition which has been recognized, namely, that discussions in the -privy council are indeed privy only to the members of the council itself. In fact, the very word "privy" indicates the nature of those discussions.

On the other han-d, the Prime Minister refers to a change which took place in the procedure some years ago. It was, in fact, Mr. Lloyd George who for the first time permitted anyone outside of the actual membership in the -council to be present; 'and he permitted a secretary of the -council to keep the memoranda to which the Prime Minister has referred. There has always been the recognized principle that, until many years afterwards, and the government itself decided that the reasons for secrecy had disappeared, those memoranda would not -be disclosed. I point out, however, that there is a distinction to be drawn between disclosure of the discussions which take place in the meetings of the council, and the result of those discussions-. I submit that the oath of office to which the Prime Minister has referred is one that applies strictly to the discussions in the meetings of the council, but not to the result of those discussions, upon which some subsequent action may be taken.
In this -case we are dealing with a directive which produces- a positive result outside of the privy council. It produces a result -precisely the same as that produced in other cases by order in council. Most certainly the rules of secrecy referred to by the Prime Minister do not apply to orders in council. That is one of the most clearly established rules that this house has insisted upon recognizing. An order in council is the result of secret discussions which must not be disclosed, but the order in -council becomes a functional interpretation of those secret discussions, which then produces action in accordance with those discussions.
This directive under a particular section of the Canada Shipping Act is in precisely the same category and is, I submit, under no greater measure of protection as to secrecy than is an order in council itself. In fact I submit it would produce a highly improper situation if simply by the device of not having a written directive and relying on an oral directive, we were then to be told that we could not know what the considerations were which produced such an- extraordinary result as that which followed in this particular case. Here we have a situation where most important provisions of the C-anada Shipping Act were waived so that ships could be operated, contrary to those provisions, in distant waters. If this principle is to apply to a directive of that kind, then the terms of secrecy might be extended to all the acts of the government made as a result of discussions in cabinet council, and the house would be left in ignorance with regard to some of the most important things that the government might do.

I therefore suggest that the Prime Minister should reconsider the decision he has made. With regret I wish also to indicate in advance that I would certainly feel that we should vote against any decision which would indicate acceptance of that point of view.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DIRECTIVE OF CABINET COUNCIL AUTHORIZING EXEMPTION FROM PROVISIONS OF SHIPPING ACT
speechtext:
I wish to make only a brief reply. The leader of the opposition says -and he is quite right-that orders in council are not covered by the oath of office. They are published, and they are regularly tabled. The practice has now been established of producing every month a summary of the orders in council passed during the previous month.
In connection with these other matters, may I say that the effective act is the act of the minister. When he consults his colleagues beforehand he does so for courtesy reasons, because of the fact that his act will involve the responsibilities of his colleagues; but the official act is the act which he performs as minister, and that act was the exemption which he granted.
The government must insist on its obligation to the crown to maintain secret the decisions made, the opinions expressed and the debates which take place in council, otherwise than through the production of orders in council or the production of the official acts of the individual ministers under the statutory powers they are exercising.

National Housing Act
that it would not be difficult to have parliament deal with any changes needed from time to time in so important a matter as the interest rate. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I shall endeavour to do just that. But you realize, sir, that it is one of the most frustrating things in the world for a member of parliament to come into this house year after year after year, representing a nation in which nature abounds with resources, and find the government sitting here twiddling its thumbs and failing to solve the problems which obviously it can solve physically, and pretending that the reason why it cannot solve the problems has to do with finance. If there is anything that could be more appropriate than discussion of finance in connection with the problem of housing, I must say that on the spur of the moment I cannot think of it. However, I will close this discussion promptly.
A valuable comment upon this whole Bradbury experiment, which I believe hon. members who are following me-and a number are

will desire to hear about, is to be found in another book by the same Dr. William A. Shaw, entitled "The Theory and Principles of Central Banking," copyrighted in 1930, after this great student of money had had time to give four years of further study to the Whole Bradbury situation.

Since I have referred to Dr. Shaw, I think it would be well for me to give the house some idea just how big a man Dr. Shaw is. In the first place, he is a doctor of letters; he is editor of the calendar of treasury-records at His Majesty's public records office; he is the author of "The History of Currency," "English Monetary Writers," '.'Currency, Credit, and the Exchanges During the Great War," "The Coming Reaction:	by Legislator," and so on. I
believe those qualifications give everyone justification for listening to his words with at least a moderate amount of attention. May I read a comment in this 1930 volume on the whole Bradbury question; it will be found at page 50:
It was only by accident during the great war that Great Britain stumbled upon the true principles of paper money issues. In the first financial shock caused by the outbreak of war the British treasury offered to the banks the help of an emergency loan currency for which the banks should pay interest. They unanimously declined to avail themselves of such form of relief, and thereupon the treasury offered to sell them currency notes at full face price without limit, and at the same time opened a currency note redemption fund for the purpose of retiring the issue as soon as the need for it was over. To the treasury's surprise the currency note quickly struck root, and proved itself completely acceptable, and gradually the treasury realized that the whole circulation of the country could be changed over to paper and the gold withdrawn. The change-over was accomplished with astonishing ease and speed by 1916. By the restrictions which were later placed on the movement of gold this currency note circulation became virtually inconvertible, though it was not declared so by law until 1925.
To this currency note circulation there was at first no limit fixed. It could fall or rise unhampered, according to the community's demand or need for it, and in the remaining years of the war and of the armistice period it bore the strain of increased prices and enormously increased production without friction or effort. For the first time in history the world had a sample of a truly automatic currency, issued only by the state, sold only at full face value, supplied or retired in complete accordance and response to the community's unfettered demand or need.
After ten years of illuminating experience this perfect, uncontrolled, and uncontrollable automatic currency system was thrown over, the automatic principle was surrendered, and our currency, although declared by law to be inconvertible paper, was placed, or was supposed to be placed, under the control of the Bank of England, and became once again sensitive, or was supposed to be made sensitive, to the vagaries of a fluctuating gold cover fund. Why was this retrograde step taken, and why did England thus throw over the pure theory of currency issue, which she had accidentally discovered and so wonderfully exemplified to the world?
The answer is threefold.
(1) The financial mind of London, both in the treasury and in the city, never assimilated the currency note concept, nor ever grasped the pure theory of currency issue which it exemplified. To this day the assertion is still made that the rise of prices which occurred during the war and armistice period was due to the currency note as an
National Housing Act
inflationary agent; whereas, in fact, the direct opposite was the case. The rise in prices preceded and caused the increase of the currency, and exactly the same increase of prices occurred in the United States, which was throughout on the freely acting gold standard, as in the United Kingdom under the currency note. It was only on the continent of Europe and in countries where the currency system was neither the free gold system of the United States of America, nor the self-regulating paper system of Great Britain, that price movements occurred of so abnormal a nature as to be attributable to currency inflation.

Before third reading is given I should like to say just a word. It will not take me too long.
I sat in the house yesterday and heard the speeches that were given on the second reading of this bill. I could not help but draw one conclusion. As I listened to these speeches the minister was reminded of things that he already knew. He was reminded of the importance of housing to the welfare of the family; that housing consisted of a material house, but within the house there lives a family making up what is known as the home. I think we sometimes get confused in our terminology, and perhaps that confusion is designed. We talk of home owners. They do not own homes; they own houses. The home is the institution that lives within the house. Housing is important therefore by reason of the fact that it contributes to the welfare of the home, or it could very easily contribute to the delinquency of family life.
We are told that the three great institutions in the world are the home, the school and the church. We usually say that, and place the home first. When it comes to caring for the welfare of the people in terms of home and family life, the policy of the government is contained within the strict confines of its monetary policy. We cannot do this and we cannot do that. No matter how desirable it is to the welfare of the people, or no matter how physically possible it is, we cannot do it because of some sort of financial restrictions. Therefore I am to conclude-I cannot help but conclude-that the policy of the government is more concerned with the perpetuation of an iniquitous, evil monetary policy or system than it is concerned with the welfare of the people.
I will simply conclude by saying that the financial brains of the government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) if you want to pool those brains and put them within his skull-

In his monetary policy the Minister of Finance is contributing to the perpetuation and the strengthening of a great Frankenstein that will break itself, and is in the process of breaking itself, and in that process will break the people and the nation; in his financial policy he is just as much a slave to the dictates of that Frankenstein as any slave was to the lash of the taskmaster's whip. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I obtained a copy of the bill from the distribution office just before coming into the house at eleven o'clock. In a matter of this kind, anxious as we are to co-operate in furthering the business of the house, and always recognizing the difficulty of pushing ahead with legislation in these days when we are sitting long hours, as well as the difficulty of having legislation printed in time for hon. members to review it, the inadequate notice we have had as to the provisions of this bill is most regrettable, measured in the light of its importance.
Yesterday we discussed the general scheme when the resolution was before the house, and I do not propose to retrace that ground at this time. However, in the limited time at my disposal I propose to make a brief review of the contents of the bill, and to offer some observations in regard to it.
I am sure the house will be glad to see a bill dealing with this subject, but I think it will view with disappointment the fact that the bill maintains a rigid formula, and is even more ungenerous toward municipalities than most of us had understood during the discussion on the resolution. After a review of the bill it can only be said that the provision made here for grants to municipalities is not only ungenerous but niggardly.
What is the scheme of the bill? No crown property, no property of any agent of the crown, whether incorporated or otherwise, is submitted to taxation at the hands of a

municipality. What is provided here is authority to the minister to make grants within certain very narrow provisions laid down in the bill.
Then, as to the way the scheme seems to work out, one progresses from one limitation to another. In the first place, in reckoning the value of crown-owned property in a municipality, the first thing done by the crown is to eliminate a great deal of such property. The crown eliminates:
(i)	real property forming part of an undertaking in respect of the conservation, irrigation, reclamation, rehabilitation or reforestation of land,
(ii)	a park, historical site, monument, museum, public library or art gallery,
(iii)	an improvement to land or structure that is not a building designed for the shelter of people, plant or movable property,
(iv)	real property under the control, management or administration of the national railways as defined in the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933, or a corporation, company, commission, board1 or agency established to perform a function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada, or
(v)	real property leased by His Majesty to a tenant from whom, by reason of such tenant's interest in that real property, a municipal taxing authority may collect real estate tax.
So we make those five deductions first of all from the value of real property owned by the crown or its agencies in municipalities.
The next such deduction is to remove from the total of crown-owned property, federal property that does not accept from a municipality any service referred to in the following terms: a service that-
(a)	the municipality customarily furnishes to real property in the municipality: and
(b)	is, in the opinion of the minister, a material service.
That is another far-reaching limitation, because if we take out of the total of federal properties those which have services only in respect of public roads and sidewalks, we have taken out of the category of properties with which the granting provisions of this bill are concerned, a great deal of property.
The third limitation is that the total of all such properties-that is to say, having eliminated all those properties in the sections I have referred to up to the present time, of which there are approximately seven categories-must exceed four per cent of the taxable property of a municipality, including that portion of the crown-owned property remaining after the subtraction of the properties in the seven categories I have mentioned.
So that unless the property survives all those tests there can be no benefit to the municipality whatsoever. But, sir, even at that point there is a fourth limitation that enters into account. It is this: that the minister is under no obligation to accept the valuation placed upon a property by a municipality.

Under this bill he retains virtually unlimited power to set the value that is to be put upon the crown property after reducing it by the elimination of property in the seven categories I have mentioned. Therefore 'he is going to have a perfectly free hand in establishing the values of crown property.
If the property survives all these limitations, a grant may be made. If you examine the provisions in regard to the grant you will see that in the first place it is not equivalent, even as applied to the limited value of crown property remaining after these various deductions have been made, to the rate of taxation as applied to other property in the municipality. The formula that is applied to determine the grant in lieu of taxes is equivalent to seventy-five per cent of the rate applicable to other property in the municipality.
The sixth hurdle in this sequence is that if the minister still chooses he is not under any obligation to make a grant on the foregoing basis. He may decide instead simply to pay for the services furnished to the crown property. In determining the amount to be fixed for the services, the minister still has a free hand. It is for him to determine what value shall be placed upon the services received or what deductions shall be made from the grant by reason of services that the minister considers the crown does not require at the hands of the municipality.
Then we come to the seventh obstacle in the sequence. Even if some municipality survives these six tests with respect to crown-owned property within its confines, the minister may still refuse to make any grant at all. There is no obligation upon the minister under this bill to make a grant even in those circumstances. The bill specifically and expressly provides that no right is conferred. If any hon. member attaches importance to the words "the minister may . . . out of moneys provided by parliament, make a grant to the municipality" and construes these words as imperative and the equivalent of "shall", I would point out that the draftsman of the bill has taken great care to make it clear that the word "may" means "may" and not "shall".

speechtext:
I think I can conclude
briefly, Mr. Speaker. Prior to the luncheon recess I was stressing the fact that as the bill is drawn it sets up a series of hurdles or obstacles in the way of municipalities qualifying for the grant. The whole emphasis is placed upon the erection of obstacles in the path of municipalities seeking any assistance from the federal government, regardless of the extent to which ownership by the federal government of property located within the municipality reduces the total of assessable property upon which the municipality may levy its needed taxes.
Just prior to the noon recess it was suggested that this represents a great improvement. I take issue with any suggestion that this bill makes any great improvement in the relations between the federal government and the municipalities in reference to the exemptions now enjoyed by this government. It is true that the introduction of this limited method of assistance is some improvement over the system which prevailed prior to 1950, under which the municipalities received nothing; but I think the argument is quite untenable, as one hon. member argued this morning, that this bill represents a great improvement. All that was paid by way of assistance to the municipalities under this grant last year was $1,578,251.13, and by no stretch of the imagination can it be said that there was any very tangible assistance given them. All that is contemplated for the present year is a modest increase to $1,800,000.
I have already indicated that having regard to the extent of federally-owned property in this city, and the very high cost of municipal services, Ottawa is not receiving sufficient assistance from the federal government.

I am glad to hear the hon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I do not think there is anything great about it. If it is an improvement, it is a very modest improvement over an even more modest ancestor.
What is the extent of the assistance? If hon. members will look at the statement at page 4224 of Hansard for Monday, June 18, they will see that the ordinary grants under the four per cent formula, which is now to be carried into this legislation, provided only eighteen municipalities with a total of just $1,389,929.41. Then six western municipalities received grants in lieu of taxes on government grain elevators aggregating $74,186.80. Five municipalities received transitional grants respecting newly acquired properties totalling $1,663.19, and twenty-two municipalities received grants in lieu of special assessments for local improvements amounting to $112,471.73. Those four subtotals make up the grand total of $1,578,251.13. If that can be called great by any stretch of the imagination, all I have to say is that I do not understand the meaning of the word. I should say that as compared with nothing before, that is a very attenuated attempt at a beginning; and to assert now that, because we are being asked to appropriate $200,000 more this year than was available for these grants last year, that is a great improvement, suggests to me, as I said this morning, that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) is just viewing this proposal through a magnifying glass.
This bill does not make any attempt to draw certain distinctions which with great respect I think might well be drawn in an approach to a matter of this kind. The four per cent formula, hedged around as it is with such a multiplicity of hurdles and obstacles, is a test that is far too rigid and exacting. I believe there must be some test, some yardstick applied; I do not suggest that the grant should be simply decided by the minister in every case without due regard for some established yardstick. But the yardstick that has been selected here, it seems to me, fails to take account of some aspects of the matter which I think should be taken into consideration.
As I mentioned yesterday, there is the fact that in many cases property owned by the crown in the right of the dominion is not used simply for the purpose of rendering a service to the people of the municipality. In

many cases it is put to a revenue-producing use; yet there is no attempt in this bill to recognize that fact. Nor is there any attempt to recognize the fact that frequently a use made of property by an agency of the crown may be directly competitive with the interests of persons who are taxpayers in the municipality. In fairness I should say I believe there is some hope of adjustment there, in that certain of the crown agencies mentioned by the minister yesterday are to be invited by the government to make grants to the municipalities in lieu of taxes. But if you examine the formula by which these crown agencies, whether corporate or otherwise, are to be guided in arriving at the amount of the grant they should make in lieu of taxes, the minister goes no further than to say it is to be fair and reasonable. As a yardstick that is just about as vague as anything could be. Unless the government goes further and lays down the rule that these corporate emanations of the crown should pay, in respect of property owned and occupied by them in these municipalities, the same rate that they would pay if they were private taxpayers, then justice will not be done to the municipalities in respect of those grants.
I cannot find any warrant for some of the other fine distinctions drawn in this bill, especially in the matter of services. The bill rejects services rendered by the municipality by way of building roads and sidewalks, and they do not enter into the calculations of the Minister of Finance in arriving at the grants to municipalities. Surely that is drawing too fine a line; that is grossly unfair to the municipality, especially in the light of the fact that the costs of municipal services have been rising to such prodigious heights in recent years.
One can only express regret, Mr. Speaker, that the emphasis placed in this bill is negative, that the whole stress put upon the bill is upon the negative features and the difficulties put in the way of municipalities seeking to qualify to receive even the modest amounts provided here. The first requirement, it seems to me, is an altogether fresh and realistic approach to the problems of these municipalities. We would like the Minister of Finance to do something to assist at that very important level of government. This bill, I am sorry to say, will contribute very little to the accomplishment of that worthy purpose.

speechtext:
I shall be brief, Mr. Speaker, but I would not want this house or the people of Canada to think that the people of Ottawa do not appreciate what is being done in this bill, nor on the other hand to believe that they are fully
Municipal Grants Act
satisfied with what they are receiving. I believe we should put first things first. Some years ago the city of Ottawa was receiving nothing. It was difficult, and it took time, to convince the people at large in the Dominion of Canada and the members in the House of Commons that the municipalities which had public buildings of the government of Canada within their boundaries should receive any special grant. The first grant given to the city of Ottawa was for the sum of $100,000. It was given by means of a vote from year to year, and a few years ago it was raised to $300,000.
Under this formula, which is rather complicated and which is incorporated in a statute, the city of Ottawa has received $962,000 for this year. That is. more than three times the amount received in the previous year. The formula was arrived at by mutual understanding. I would not want this house to think there are any serious differences between the assessors of the city of Ottawa and the assessors who act on behalf of the government of Canada. There is, however, one point on which there is disagreement, and that is that the formula allows only seventy-five per cent of the excess over four per cent to be taxable at the public school rate for the city of Ottawa.
Nevertheless under this formula the city of Ottawa is certain of a fixed sum based on the assessment from year to year. I only wanted to point out that if anyone wishes to say this is a niggardly sum or that there has been no improvement, certainly the people of Ottawa do not feel that way. They are looking forward to improvement in the formula, and to an increased grant as the development of the city progresses. There is one thing that should be remembered, and that is that the city of Ottawa also receives some benefits from grants made to the federal district commission. Again there is agreement between the city and the federal district commission. I am sure that the government and the members at large look upon the city of Ottawa as a national capital and will be only too glad to approve this legislation. Perhaps they can improve it, as I have suggested, by making a grant to the full one hundred per cent instead of the seventy-five per cent.

speechtext:
As I
listened to the member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) I was reminded of the biblical parable of the poor man who was satisfied with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. It would seem to me that his point of view was that of the poor man who was grateful for any crumbs which fell from the rich man's table, even though now those crumbs may seem to be like crusts of bread.

Municipal Grants Act

speechtext: I am glad you consider a million dollars a crumb.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I believe that parable
well represents the point of view expressed. Actually in the past that has been very much ' the position of the municipalities in their relationship to the federal government. In recent years the federal government has been prepared to pass out a few crumbs to the municipalities, and some, not all, of the municipalities have been grateful for those few crumbs.
The thing we have overlooked in this discussion is that Ottawa is not the only city concerned with this bill. In considering the bill I should like to emphasize the note which the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) struck in his concluding remarks, concerning the importance of government at the municipal level in any democratic system. The tendency here seems to be to underestimate the importance of municipal government. Any services that a municipal government can render to a community should be rendered by the municipality because that government is closest to the people. The further removed any government is from the people, the less efficient that government is likely to be. In a democratic system we must not take any measures that will remove from the municipalities the responsibilities for those phases of government which they can render best.
In recent years the municipalities have found they have not sufficient income to meet many of the responsibilities which are theirs to perform. Their field of taxation is pretty well limited to real property, and is probably the most limited of all levels of government. We saw that in the depression. It was not the federal government or the provincial governments who went into bankruptcy, but scores and scores of municipalities across this country found themselves going into bankruptcy. We, and other individuals, hesitate to render very much aid to education. We still leave the cost of education to be borne largely by municipal governments. There is a fear that, if the federal government put too much money into education, in some way they will have a voice in the curriculum and in the administration of the school system. I should never want to see in this country an educational system whereby all financial responsibility for it was removed from municipal governments. Those countries in which educational costs have been centralized and have been borne entirely by central governments have shown us that there is always a tendency for the local people to lose interest in their schools; and what applies to the school system applies

to many of the other services that the municipalities render. My point is that municipal government is so important in a democratic system that we must do nothing to undermine government at that particular level.
In the past it was taken for granted that crown properties should be exempt from taxation. But gradually over the years the federal government has adopted the practice, as I mentioned at first, of giving a few handouts to the municipalities. This bill provides for nothing more than larger handouts by the federal government to the municipalities. The amount that the municipality is to receive in lieu of taxes for federal properties is still largely left to a matter of dickering between the municipality and the federal government. That, I submit, is just not good business practice. There is only one way in which this matter can be handled properly in the interests of the municipality and in the interests of good democratic government. The federal property should be assessed on the same basis as is any other property in the municipality and the federal government should expect to pay municipal taxes on that property on exactly the same basis as does any other property owner in the municipality. If the federal government has reason to believe that the assessment is too high or that it is unfair, it has the opportunity-as has any other taxpayer in the community- of going before a board and there arriving at a fair assessment. So long as the question of payment in lieu of taxation is left as it is, a matter of negotiation between municipalities and the federal government, so long will you have discrimination. You are opening the door there for political patronage on the municipal level, just as we find political patronage existing within other services at the present time.
Government buildings or government offices are placed in certain municipalities, certain towns and cities, because in the opinion of the federal government authorities that is the centre from which those offices can best serve the community, the province or the country at large. As to Ottawa, I do not think Ottawa as a city had a great deal to say about whether or not this should be the national capital. Ottawa was chosen as the national capital because it was felt that this was the one place in Canada that would best serve such a purpose at the time when the selection was made. Whether the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) and other Ottawa members are quite content with the handout that Ottawa gets from year to year-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: He did not say that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
-is not a matter of importance. It is neither here nor there as

far as the discussion of this bill is concerned. Whether or not the people of Ottawa are satisfied is probably another question. But whether the municipality concerned be Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal or the smallest municipality in this country, I can see no good reason why the federal government should not be required to pay taxes on all federal property, assessed by the same method as are other properties in the municipality.
There was, of course, a day when municipalities thought that there was some advantage in getting a government office or a government building established within the municipality. There were benefits. There are, of course, benefits which accrue to any municipality; but there are also responsibilities and there are also services. It is to the certain advantage of a city or town that any industrial enterprise should be established in that city or town; but because the city or town is going to derive some benefit from the establishment there of the industry or commercial enterprise is no good reason why the citizens of the city or town should give that enterprise property tax-free in perpetuity. That practice is being rapidly abandoned. Cities and towns which in times past sought to attract industrial enterprises by granting exemption from taxation have come to change their point of view; and today the general practice is that even those enterprises which at one time were considered to render to the municipality sufficient service to warrant exemption from taxation are being taxed today. There is an increasing demand that all such properties should bear their fair share of municipal taxation. I think it would be difficult for anyone to give good, sound, logical reasons why the citizens of any particular municipality should be called upon to support a federal government office or building which serves not only the municipality but, in some cases, the country, in other cases the province and in still other cases the surrounding countryside.
There is another feature to be considered. Actually what the government is doing in this bill is merely passing on to the municipalities what they have taken from them by reason of government policy which has led to the present rising cost of living. Within the last year every municipality in this country has had to raise its tax rate because of the rising cost of living which has resulted from this government's policy. Many municipalities have had to step up their tax rate as much as twenty mills owing to the rising costs of material and services. For that this government's policy is to a large extent responsible. In increasing the size of the
Municipal Grants Act
handout that the government are giving to the municipalities by this bill, they are simply handing back to the municipalities all or part of what they have taken from them as a result of their policy which led to that rising cost of material and general living. In the light of the importance of municipal government, and in fairness to all municipalities, because so long as this present system is followed there is bound to be a certain degree of unfairness as between municipality and municipality, the question of the taxes the federal government should pay on any government piece of property in a municipality should not be left to negotiation so that some municipalities can get a better deal or drive a harder bargain with the federal government than others. It should be on a straight assessment basis, and the federal government pay their taxes as other taxpayers in the country.

I am

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: Small town mentality.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
In his remarks he referred to the modest little house in which I happen to live on Island Park drive, which he referred to as millionaires' row. I am afraid he does not know his geography in Ottawa

Municipal Grants Act
very well. Certainly, the one millionaire's row we have here-and he has probably driven around it and seen the great estates- is in Rockcliffe, where the true millionaires of this town live. I gather their taxes are very very low. I think probably he has inadvertently put his finger on one of the main difficulties in the Ottawa taxation situation. It is the fact that our Ottawa city council has seen fit to acquire large sections of adjoining townships and have left out this one very desirable location, which contains people who are able to pay very heavy taxes. They have been left out of the scheme of things here.
That Ottawa has not taken in Rockcliffe is one of the factors contributing to the very high rate of taxation here. I notice that some of the newspapers have mentioned that for the first time a member of parliament from other than Ottawa ridings has taken some interest in the taxation problems of Ottawa. That may be a fair comment, but let me point out to them that I was trying to do a service to the other hon. members here, because after all we as members represent the city of Ottawa as well as our own constituencies. I was trying to point out to the other hon. members that from my own personal experience, and from the experience of other hon. members who have found it necessary to purchase homes in Ottawa, we have suddenly become very conscious of the difficulties with which the taxpayers of Ottawa are faced in meeting this terrifically high municipal taxation that is in effect in this town.
It just appears to me, as I said in my remarks during the discussion on the resolution stage, that Ottawa is in effect, by virtue of the fact that most people living here are civil servants, a company town; and it seems to me that we as members of parliament, and indeed the government, should be very much concerned with the welfare of our employees, just as we would expect any company which was running a company town to be concerned with the welfare of its employees.
I realize that at the present time the government probably has not the power, but I would suggest that it might be a very worthwhile thing for this government to consider asking the citizens of Ottawa or the council of Ottawa whether they would not consider having one of the keener minds on our treasury board associated with them on their board of control. We feel, in addition, that their action in bringing in this legislation and incorporating this principle in a bill to become the law of the country is a further step forward. Certainly I agree with the hon. members for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) in the remarks they have made concerning the effect of the bill.
The minister, in discussing the matter at the resolution stage, dealt at some length with one of the main points which I shall discuss briefly this afternoon. His observations appear at page 4224 of Hansard where he states that he made it quite clear in his statement of November 14, 1949, which was the original negotiation announcement of this policy, that the crown must reserve to itself the right to establish the valuation. I do not think we can quarrel too much with that statement. The crown naturally would have to take

Municipal Grants Act
special care to see that valuations of property were done in a fair and reasonable manner. Then he went on to say:
These are ex gratia payments and, for reasons which I think are fairly obvious, the crown could not put itself entirely in the hands of the local assessors.
I agree with the minister that from the legal point of view these are ex gratia payments, but that is only from the purely legal point of view. As well as being ex gratia, these payments are ex justitia; they are based upon justice and reason.
The minister went on to describe arrangements which would be made for agreement between the federal government and local assessors, and pointed out that in one or two cases, one of which was Halifax, the department had retained outside advisers to assist in coming to a conclusion.
The city of Halifax is appreciative of the efforts made to reach a fair and equitable settlement in the matter, so far as grants to Halifax are concerned. However, I am' sure the minister is fully aware that only the first step has been taken. We hope that it is not just the first step and that in the next few years as this legislation becomes more familiar and as we get used to its administration there will be room for adjustments which the cities and municipalities think should be made.
I think the government has been right in drawing up the bill in the way they have. I would point out to the minister that the real test of this legislation will be the manner in which it is administered. I am sure that he will give special attention to matters of that kind which will be coming up in the future.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) suggested that this bill would open the door to political patronage at the municipal level. The hon. member is bringing to my attention the fact that $53.66 is also being paid to Maple Ridge, but I mentioned that. This legislation is mainly due to two hon. members from British Columbia. Some years ago the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) introduced a resolution along these very lines. He is now in a more fortunate position to bring about legislation of this kind. As long as he listens to some of my advice he will help to bring about legislation that may be of assistance.
The other hon. member who has assisted in this is the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). If I understood correctly what he said, he was contending that government properties should be subject to regular assessment and pay taxation at the regular rate. I agree entirely with that. I can see no reason why government property should not be assessed in the normal manner and taxed at the regular rates.
When I first came to Ottawa the grant being made to this city, if I remember correctly, was $100,000. At that time I sat where the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) now sits. I objected strenuously to that grant being made. But I had the privilege of visiting Washington, the great capital of the United States, and I saw what the forty-eight states had done to build up the capital of that country. I began to realize that Ottawa was not the capital of Ontario, it was the capital of the dominion, and I was ready to agree to an increased grant. I repeat that government properties should be subject to regular assessment and taxation just the same as any other business or residential property.
If this city is the capital of Canada I contend that its form of government should be similar to that of Washington, D.C. I do not want to say anything derogatory about the local government of Ottawa, but I might mention that in Vancouver, the third city of

Canada with a population of some 400,000, there are only eight aldermen and no controllers. You would need to be a mathematician or a member of the Department of Finance to keep track of the number of controllers and aldermen in this little town, of 135,000 people.
If the people of Canada are to put up the money, as I believe they should, to make this the most beautiful capital on the North American continent, then they should be protected by a form of government similar to that in Washington rather than the present government. Whenever you pick up either the Journal or the Citizen you see where Charlotte and Tardif are quarrelling over a pinball game or something else, and all the time we are putting up the money. I disagree strongly with that idea. I do not care whether Charlotte and Tardif like it or do not like it; if they come out to British Columbia we will show them how to run a great city without government assistance.
I want to come back to these figures. It is easy for the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) or for the hon. member for Vancouver North-I should correct that and say "Coast-Capilano"; they gave up a good name and took on a poorer one-to argue as they have, but I think something should be said in fairness to the minister and the system he is trying to bring into effect.
In my riding is located the largest army camp in western Canada. The government has been criticized over that camp, even by the people of Chilliwack. That camp has now been set up as a permanent army camp to form part of our national defence. Its payroll contributes largely to the welfare of the district. Many people criticized the government for taking four or five hundred acres out of taxation.
Within two miles or so of where I live is one of the finest airports in the Dominion of Canada comprising 900 acres. I have in my office, from the days when I used to be a member of the municipal council, a file filled with criticisms of the federal government and the Department of National Defence because there would be no taxes received from these 900 acres of what had not been very profitable land-I will put it that way. For the last five years some 900 children within my own district would not have had the benefit of education of any kind but for the facilities of that camp. During the disastrous floods of 1948 the people who had to be evacuated would have had nowhere to go if it had not been for the facilities at that airport. In the plans now being formulated for the evacuation of civilians from Vancouver and New Westminster in the event of bombing, it is planned to have evacuees handled at this airport.
Municipal Grants Act
I am saying this to point out to those in my own riding that it is not simply a question of saying they have lost the municipal revenue from some 900 acres of land. They must not forget what they have gained through the facilities at the Abbotsford airport in the way of education for their children, accommodation during the floods of 1948 and so on. The same applies to the Chilliwack army camp. However, I do not think the minister has gone far enough. The present formula is a step in the right direction, but eventually these grants should be made in every municipality, regardless of size. That should apply whether it is the great city of Ottawa, the lesser city of Halifax, or even the little area out here called Carleton, where the residents apparently have to walk 200 yards to get their mail, which I admit is a great drawback and hardship, particularly when you consider some of the speeches they have to carry home with them. However, I agree with those hon. members who have suggested that there is only one proper formula to be applied in connection with the taxation of this property; that is, government property should be assessed and taxed in exactly the same way as other property, with the same right of appeal to the assessment courts or other civilian courts.

speechtext:
I might remind hon. gentlemen, including the hon. member for Fraser Valley, that Carleton county now embraces a very substantial part of the city of Ottawa, so I am speaking also for one segment of this city. It should be remembered that we are dealing with what was regarded simply as a temporary expedient to meet a situation everyone recognized had to be faced in some way. The hon. member for Ottawa East said he thought there had been little disagreement as to the assessment of the property in question. That is correct. As I understand, there has been no disagreement. I also understand it has been agreed that the buildings in the city of Ottawa owned and operated by the Canadian government, other than the parliament buildings themselves, should be assessed at a figure which, if taxes were paid in the ordinary way, would have produced during the past year a tax of $3,338,900, as compared with the $962,392 the city received. Certainly $962,392 is not an insignificant figure; nevertheless we must appreciate that any payment, no matter how large or small it may be, is adequate or inadequate in relation to the figure for which it is substituted.
It has been pointed out that in this city other payments are made, and also that certain other services are rendered by the dominion government in connection with policing and activities of that kind. Of course those are not in substitution for the local responsibilities in that respect. The city of Ottawa carries on all the ordinary functions and responsibilities of a city of this size. The figure being paid, therefore, must be related to what would be received from those buildings were they not operated by the government. Making full allowance for any services that are rendered, comparing the $962,392 with the $3,338,900 which would have been received from those buildings on a normal assessment rate and normal taxes,
[Mr. Drew.l
then I say that without question the amount being paid to the city of Ottawa, the capital of Canada, is not adequate to give the city a fair return for the taxes it is compelled to give up in relation to those buildings.
Having 'said that, I want to point out that there are buildings which fall into different categories, and in discussing this whole subject we must remember that fact. For instance, as has been pointed out by some hon. members, there are buildings that are definite attractions from the tourist point of view. Others, while perhaps providing no utility service or no revenue service, might be placed in a special category. They are only a relatively small part of the buildings or operations under consideration. Then there are those operations which are of particular service to the community, such as post offices and buildings of that kind. Those should be placed in a special category, and some return made for the property set aside for those purposes. There is a third category, and that is the category to which the consideration of the members of this house must be directed, whether or not we at this time deal with that subject in any effective way. In that category come those buildings and those activities, industrial or otherwise, which operate on a revenue producing basis and which should pay taxes the same as any similar activity.
At a time when the government is extending its activities into many fields for defence production, in the form of crown companies and otherwise, this is something which must be faced. It certainly is not fair to any community, and all communities in Canada depend largely or in many cases almost entirely upon taxes obtained from real estate, to take over large areas in those communities, whether they be urban or rural municipalities, calling for the services that are necessary in such an area, policing, educational and others, and then not pay the normal tax rate for the property. I can think of many extremely important undertakings which were opened up during the last world war which caused great difficulties for the municipalities in which they were located. The people of those municipalities would have been the very last to have expressed any wish that those operations or undertakings should not go forward in the area. Nevertheless they did face great difficulties as a result of what was done.
Take as an example the great explosives plant at Ajax. This called for a large tract of land, not only for the explosives plant but also for the houses required for the

43G7
workers who went to that new and segregated community. Under the general provision that governments do not pay taxes, almost insurmountable problems were created in regard to educational and other facilities of that nature. Then in the case of the very large aircraft development at Malton, great areas were set aside for the plant and still larger areas to house the workers who came there to take part in that production. Again that area certainly welcomed a development of that kind, but it created immense difficulties. Since that time special steps have been taken and it has been possible to meet these particular problems, but that redress cannot begin to take care of all cases of that kind. Once again we are confronted with the necessity of a large expansion of defence production. Once again it will be necessary for the government to take over new tracts of land or acquire additional land in areas where there is already production of that type. I am satisfied that some steps must be taken to meet such a situation.
As for the bill which is before us, it is simply a bill to interpret in statutory form the order in council which introduced this device last year. As has been pointed out by some of the members, there does not yet appear to be any clear reason why four per cent happens to be the figure of concentration which becomes the starting point for taxes of this kind. Without in any way reflecting on the motives which prompted the remarks of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), it is perhaps easy to understand why he regards with a greater measure of approval this hit or miss system, and that is all it is, than might the members from other communities of a similar size. Halifax receives the second largest payment of any city in Canada. As compared with Ottawa, which received $962,392, the city of Halifax receives $208,489.93. I have no doubt that the city of Halifax should receive that, and probably a great deal more. However, that is a very substantial payment in comparison with the city of Vancouver, for instance which receives a total under these various types of payment of $172.12. There will not be any suggestion that there are not large government operations in the city of Vancouver which should be contributing their share, and which are earning revenues which could provide some contribution to the ordinary services maintained by the city of Vancouver.
It is noticeable that neither the city of Montreal nor the city of Toronto receives any payment under this. It is all very well to make facetious remarks about cities such as
Municipal Grants Act
Montreal and Toronto not deserving any payments, but the fact is that if a system is sound every city should be dealt with on the same basis.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I will admit that it was introduced during the second year that I happened to be premier of that province; and that is the same law that is in force today.
'Mr. Drew.]
In any event, when there is any division as between federal and provincial governments, I am quite prepared to have my remarks apply to the principle involved, and I do not wish to have any qualifications in regard to that principle, whether it be at the provincial or at the federal level. I am satisfied that as governments-whether they be federal, provineial or municipal-go into the operation and ownership of properties which earn revenue, those properties should pay taxes on exactly the same level as will any other property in those communities. I believe in free enterprise. I believe in free enterprise being protected against specially-subsidized government operations in the same field. In many of these cases governments are getting into operations where they compete with these organizations which, as ordinary corporations, must pay taxes. I am satisfied that it is in the interests of good government and of efficiency of operation to have those organizations pay taxes which put them on the same competitive level as any other organization in the same field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow another question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt him, but does he know whether or not the Ontario hydro pays municipal taxes on its installations?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: They do not, on the same level. But may I also say that they have been making certain special allowances to the municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: But on the reasoning that my hon. friend was adopting, they should pay taxes on the same basis.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: I thought I had made it clear that I asked that there be no reservations made in my remarks in regard to that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: That is fine.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
No matter what may have been sound in the past, I think we have come to the time when, if governments at any level are going to extend into operations which compete with ordinary operations, they should pay taxes on those operations so that they may be subject to the same tests and the same standards of efficiency as is any other operation engaged in the same business.
As to this present bill, naturally it is one of those cases where it is wise to accept whatever is put forward on a provisional basis. But I can only express regret that a method which is so unscientific and inadequate for the purpose of balancing up these payments across the country is to be perpetuated in statutory form. Nevertheless,

since the government puts this proposal forward as the means by which it is going to continue whatever payments are being made, I am making these remarks now to urge upon tne government that, in view of the fact that there is to be a second session this year, they be prepared to review this whole subject with the idea of examining this matter on the basis of some sound principle.
I would hope that they would come forward with a plan which will deal with properties of different kinds: those properties that are simply for the general service of the people of Canada, such as these buildings in which we are now meeting; those buildings which perform a special service for the locality such as post offices and buildings of that kind, and which are not operating anything in the nature of a business; and those operations that are straight business operations, operating in many cases in competition with private businesses. In that case I would hope that the government, within this present year, would be prepared to accept the principle-a principle that I regard as a sound one-that where the government goes into operations of this kind, those government operations will pay taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: Ottawa would not get much on that basis.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: I am quite prepared that Ottawa should stand on exactly the same basis as any other municipality in regard to whatever principle is applied. But I would point out again that, excluding these parliament buildings, the buildings in the city of Ottawa which are operated by the government and which are collecting revenues of various kinds, are assessed at a level which would have produced during this current year a total of $3,338,900 Instead of the $962,392 they are receiving.

Municipal Grants Act
Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank)-unless they receive a more adequate return for the number of buildings that have been taken over and are being taken over all the time.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, I have put these remarks forward recognizing the fact that we are going to have another session; seeking also to emphasize the fact that any system which only provides payment to eighteen municipalities throughout the whole of Canada in relation to government operations cannot be a sound system; and suggesting that there is no reason for this arbitrary 4 per cent basis, but that the members of this house should be called upon to consider some scientific formula which will not only be good for the present but will meet the situation which is created with the ever-increasing entry of the government into business activities and other activities of various kinds across Canada.

Skim milk for the rest of the
country. None of the 18 cities concerned begrudge the amount that Ottawa will get. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

Of course it is preserved by
the constitution. We have modified the constitution from time to time. I remember the day when you used to have to obtain a fiat if you wanted to sue the dominion government, and unless you got a fiat you were out of court. We have modified that, and

no one was particularly hurt by the result that people are getting a greater measure of justice.
To suggest that crown corporations should be invited to make contribution is wrong. It is either right or wrong. The crown corporations ought to pay taxes in the same way as everyone else pays taxes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
The argument everlastingly has been made when the municipal officials went to the provinces and asked them to pay taxes or went to the dominion and asked them to pay taxes: What difference does it make? The money is taken out of one pocket and put into another. But you take it out of different pockets. The pockets do not belong to the same people. That is the trouble. The municipalities will not even have any pants with pockets in them if you keep on refusing to pay your full share of taxes. In so far as the provincial government not paying taxes is concerned, here is an opportunity for the dominion government to set an example. After all, this is the Great White Father. We are the people who have an over-all responsibility. If we begin paying taxes on government property the municipalities will drive the provinces into the position where they will have to do the same thing.
Municipal Grants Act
It seems to me that is an excellent example of what is possible. We should have gone the whole way. It is an important matter to the municipalities. They have turned every way, trying to find a few dollars here and there, and yet on the other hand they see these large government buildings, which bring them some advantage, not paying taxes. That is a sore spot.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: Very few of them refuse those buildings.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
Of course not; why should they? They are a part of Canada-and there are decided advantages to the local people. But there are disadvantages, too. It seems to me the government might well consider going the whole way and making it easier for the municipalities, which will bring them taxes not only from the dominion but from the provinces.
I would have thought that on this occasion the government would have taken advantage of the expression of feeling in the house when the original motion was debated, and settled this matter once and for all. I do hope that in due time the minister will set an example for the provinces. The federal government is doing a very good job of educating the people in the payment of income tax. It would be good for the dominion to feel that it is paying its share, so that the municipalities will not feel that they have been donfe in by the dominion government. I do hope the minister will give consideration to the requests made here from all sides of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I for one am frank to say that I welcome the bill, and consider it a great improvement in the treatment of this subject. When I was first elected to the House of Commons in 1940 this subject was generally ignored. There was however a specific bill giving an annual grant of $100,000 to the city of Ottawa in lieu of taxes. When that bill came before the house at my first session one hon. member in the opposition put forward the proposal that it be cut off altogether, and that there should be no grant whatever. The idea was not popular, however, and out of fairness I must add that the opposition did not pursue it. Indeed the hon. member who made the proposal receded from it.
Treatment of the subject was postponed during the war years. In 1944, we were able to have a joint committee of both houses of parliament to deal with the subject. Unfortunately that committee was set up at the end of the session and its work was cut short by the termination of the session. However, it did one useful thing in that it

Municipal Grants Act
served to acquaint all hon. members with the nature of the problem, and focused it on their minds.
The grant involved in the city of Ottawa bill was increased in the following year to $300,000. In the last year there was a temporary order in council making provision for an interim payment, and today we have this bill. When I say the bill represents a great improvement I believe any hon. member who has examined developments on this subject since confederation will agree with me.
I was somewhat disappointed at the violence of the language of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) in dealing with the subject, and his attempt to hammer it into the position of being some party matter that could be bandied back and forth between the parties. I do not believe we can deal with the municipalities of this country on that basis.
Their true position is that merely of statutory creations of the various provinces. In Ontario the municipal act and the present system of municipal government were brought into legislative being by the Baldwin government in 1849, which is one hundred and two years ago. There has been no change in the principle of that legislation since that time. It has been patched up a little each year, but the basic principle has never changed.
The situation is that we have municipalities, the creatures of the provinces, saddled with responsibilities in social welfare and other fields that were never thought of one hundred and two years ago. It is a completely changed set of obligations, and all costing large sums of money. Along with this however they have had the same basis of finding revenue, namely out of the land tax on real estate. I suggest the problem is not one that can be solved by the dominion government alone. It is a very difficult one, and perhaps one the dominion government may be wise not to stress too strenuously. Provincial-municipal difficulties are very real, and we could easily do more harm than good by interfering in something outside our legislative competence and jurisdiction. While we realize where the responsibility for that problem lies-and 1 have every sympathy for provincial and municipal governments in trying to face up to it-it seems to me that there needs to be a complete revision of the jurisdiction as between municipalities and provinces, and a revision that will put the financial responsibilities now placed on the municipalities into line with their sources of revenue.
[Mr. McDraith.l
I believe that would be a common ground for almost all parties in the house, and all members who have given any real thought to the situation. It is not good enough in dealing with the subject to say, "Oh, if the dominion government pays taxes, just like any other taxpayer, the problem will be solved." It just is not that type of problem.
I for one will welcome the day when a provincial government will come forward and will really look at the municipal legislation and make an attempt to bring municipal authority and responsibility into line with municipal financial sources of revenue. When that is being done, and as part of the process, I have no doubt at all that we will have to look at the responsibility as between the dominion and provincial governments. I welcome the opportunity of doing that, and I will welcome the day when we can do it. I look forward with eagerness to that day, and I hope it may be done in my time.
I for one am not satisfied with the one-hundred-and-two-year-old system. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) dealt with the grant to Ottawa, and seemed to single it out. I do not know what view he was seeking to convey, but he did make use of some biblical references. I did not like particularly his use of biblical references as related to this subject-but that is neither here nor there. I do object strenuously however when he describes as a crumb a grant of one million dollars to a municipality trying to carry on. I suggest it is something different from that, and that a million dollars of the taxpayers' money is not a crumb either to the municipality, the dominion government or to anyone else.
I noticed today that, regardless of the position hon. members may have taken as to the adequacy or inadequacy of the bill, there is one refreshing change. There seems to be unanimity as to the idea that something should be done. It was interesting and refreshing to observe that the disagreement was only as to the details as to what and how much should be done.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), who represents the adjoining constituency, made one reference with which I am strongly in accord. He used the hydro as an example of an enterprise which was carrying on business in competition with ordinary business and not being taxed in the ordinary way. I was glad to hear the leader of the opposition make that direct and unequivocal reference to the desirability of its paying taxes as an ordinary taxpayer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt the hon. member for Ottawa West, because I

think we are in almost complete agreement on the general purposes, but I would point out that I was referring to those aspects of that commission which are in competition with other business.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: I so understood the leader of the opposition.

speechtext: I want that to be clear; I do not want to be misunderstood. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
I think there was a perfectly clear understanding of the remarks of the leader of the opposition. I am afraid that I cannot differ with him on that point. As I said, I welcome his statement. However, I was sorry to hear him use the figure obtained from the city hall about the tax the dominion government would pay-$3,339,000- because a figure taken in that way is misleading. It is not .a complete and accurate figure. The leader of the opposition gave some reason why it is not wholly accurate and there are other reasons which are quite obvious. If the dominion government paid taxes on all properties it would involve the city in providing all the services that are provided for the ordinary taxpayer.
The point I wish to make in that connection, and this point is particularly strong in my mind as a result of my work on the joint committee a few years ago, is that to arrive at a correct figure requires a good deal of detailed examination of the services being rendered and whether or not they are normal services rendered to any taxpayer, and so on. That varies sharply from one municipality to the other, as I learned in the committee. That was the sole point I wished to make in referring to it.
It is well also to realize that this matter of the dominion government making large grants to municipalities raises another implication which has been put forward here today. If you are making large grants to a municipality, are you going to have a say in the administration of its affairs? That is a question which I am sure the municipalities will wish to consider most carefully. I think it is something that ought to be foreseen.
The question of a federal district commission has been put forward in this house for many years and has received a great deal of consideration. I do not think it is relevant to a discussion of this bill, but perhaps it should be remembered that the district commission does some good work in the area that
Municipal Grants Act
is of benefit to the area as well as to the rest of Canada. These things should be considered in detail.
Then as to the amount of the grant, I seem to have troubled the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) when I said that I welcomed this bill as a great improvement. In my opinion the amount is not adequate, but at least we now have a formula upon which we can put forward representations concerning the inadequacy and what I would consider the improper allowances in computing the grant. Mention could be made, although I do not think it is relevant on the principle of this bill, as to whether one type of building should come under one subsection and so on.
