speechtext: Is it not rather violent language on the part of the hon. member to talk about these being improper allowances?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

The hon. member said
improper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: Perhaps I am subject to correction by the hon. member for Eglinton on that point. With his precision of language, he would have used the word "inadequate" instead of "improper". I am not able to define clearly when an inadequacy becomes an impropriety. You could argue about that at some considerable length. I gladly substitute the word "inadequate" for "improper" if the hon. member will find it more agreeable. Without taking more time, I believe I have expressed my views in general on the bill. I want to close with the note on which I began, and that is my appreciation to the government for at long last bringing forward this overdue bill. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for just a few minutes I should like to speak in support of the position taken on Monday by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the position taken in the house today by a number of hon. members on the government side, particularly the hon. member for Spa-dina (Mr. Croll). It seems to me that just as the federal government expects the people of Canada to pay their taxes, the federal government should come clean on this matter and pay grants equal to what would be the municipal taxes on government-owned property.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) relies strongly on section 125 of the British North America Act which reads:
No lands or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation,.

Municipal Grants Act
The hon. member for Spadina has already pointed out that until recently we had the fiction-I use that word advisedly-that the crown could not be sued without the consent of the crown, in other words without the grant of a fiat. During this session we have passed legislation doing away with that fiction. There are other fictions to be found in the British North America Act itself. For example, we have section 9 which reads:
The executive government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.
We know what that means; we understand that language, but in point of fact the authority in charge of this country consists of the ministers of the Canadian cabinet. Similarly there is section 54 which reads:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
There again is a fiction that does not bother us very much. Every time a money bill is brought in a minister stands up and says that His Excellency the Governor General recommends the bill to the consideration of the house, but never since I have been here has there been a message from the Governor General brought into this house assuring us of that fact. We know what happens, and as a matter of fact I prefer it that way; it is the government that takes the responsibility for money bills, not the person who happens to be the nominal head of the country. I emphasize the point that the exact wording of section 54 of the constitution is being completely disregarded; we treat it as a fiction. Well, if that is the case with these other sections of the British North America Act which I have cited, I think we could do the same with section 125. We need not amend it. We can leave it there and continue to claim that property belonging to Canada is not legally liable to taxation, but that need not prevent the government from making grants in lieu of municipal taxation. One might find certain classes of property such as post offices, which are in every community, and which might not be included; but apart from a very few exceptions like that it does seem to me, as the hon. member for Spadina has said, that the government should come clean and pay grants in lieu of taxes on federal property to all municipalities in which federal property is situated.
As the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) says, this four per cent formula that has been worked out is something definite. It improves the position of Ottawa,

and I for one do not begrudge that at all. But, as has been clearly pointed out, it still leaves Ottawa about $2 million short of what it would get if it received the taxation that *could be levied on all federal property in this city if they had the right to do so. In view of the unfairness of this situation to Ottawa itself, in that it does not get the full amount it should, together with the uncertainty as to the wisdom of this formula which has been expressed just as forcefully on the government side as on this side, I think the suggestion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) should be taken seriously and this bill should be laid over at least until next session.
I have heard a number of hon. members opposite express some concern about the language of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), which was referred to as strong and violent. I did not realize that his language was quite as strong as that; he did not even shout as loudly as he sometimes does. I noticed that what really exercised the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was the way the hon. member for Spadina spoke. It was not the language he used; it seemed to me it was the force of his argument that really bothered the minister. Quite frankly I feel that this legislation should not be proceeded with at this time; in fact I am rather startled that the government should ask that this bill be dealt with this session, particularly in view of the desire to get the urgent business through. I wonder why a contentious measure of this kind should be brought forward, particularly when on the basis of the order in council and an item in the estimates the various cities that have been getting these payments could continue to get them and in the meantime this matter could be given further study. I suggest in all seriousness that the minister should discuss with some of his colleagues the advisability of having one of them move the adjournment of this debate, and let this matter stand over until the fall session for further consideration, which I would hope might result in a fair deal for all our municipalities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
On a
measure as important as this I think all groups in the house should state their position. I do not like the idea of making grants to municipalities from the federal treasury, and I do not think the bill should provide for grants at all. My own view is that the municipalities of Canada ought to be able to present to the senior governments assessment notices and tax bills just as they present them to ordinary citizens. However, I concede that the British North America Act does circumscribe the federal government with

certain constitutional limitations which may necessitate a change in that act sometime in the future; but we should be looking forward to the day when that change can be made, so the municipalities will not have to come hat in hand, like a bunch of beggars, asking the federal government for a handout. That is not the right way to do business at all. Under the circumstances I think the bill is taking the wrong approach.
There is another thing I do not like about it. When we take the position we have taken in this bill we hedge our offer around with qualifications and escape clauses to the point where no one is certain what the bill means or when a municipality may have any rights. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has placed in the bill certain qualifications which, while making it appear that he is being very generous to the municipalities, make sure that the grant is not going to be established as a matter of right in any circumstances. I do not like that approach to the matter. At the same time I am prepared to admit, together with the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and various others, that it is a faltering step in the right direction. We hope the federal government will get its feet under it and be ready to take a proper step toward relieving the municipalities of the burden imposed upon them by the fact that the federal and provincial governments have very large amounts of property in those municipalities.
I am not saying that even if the terms of this bill were extended and a more generous formula applied, that would solve the problems of the municipalities. I think the hon. member for Ottawa West put his finger upon a very important point. One of the things I have had against the people of Ontario, to be quite frank, is that they have been so slow to make changes which have been proved necessary for many years.

I do; and I like Ontario very much. But even if the grant to the city of Ottawa were increased there would have to be quite a number of changes in the attitude of the city fathers here and the board of control, before they could overcome their problem. They have made a number of blunders in this city of late which have put them in a difficult position. I have been interested in studying the taxation situation in this city for some time. I note, for example, that in 1930 public school supporters in this *city paid 31-75 mills on their assessment. 'The rate continued to increase until it reached a peak of 39 mills in 1936. After remaining at that point for about four years it began to decline, until in 1945 it was back almost to where it was in 1930. Since then it has gone up every single year. The rate last year was 47i mills, and this year another substantial increase has been announced bringing it up to around 52 mills. Thus in a period of six years we have had an increase of something like 20 mills in this city. One of the blunders that I think they made here that caused a great deal of difficulty and which has placed a tremendous burden upon the taxpayers is that they bit off a whole lot more than they could chew in this annexation business. They were prompted, of course, by the federal government's great plans for a greater and more beautiful capital city for the dominion. We all agree that this capital city should be a real capital city, but we do not believe that the city should be asked or prodded by the federal government or anyone else to take steps that are too long for it to be able to keep its own balance. Now, they have done that. They went ahead and annexed in one step too much territory around the whole city. They find now that they, have to provide services for this district and are spending huge sums of money in

What is the situation now? The tax rates go up and up until, as the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) has said, the people are practically burdened down. That in itself is bound to bring a reaction in the sale value of the property as time goes by. When speaking of the member for Comox-Alberni, I am reminded that he made a rather interesting suggestion. I do not want to be tied down to them. I do not know exactly what they would be, but the generally accepted municipal services, such as garbage collection, police, fire and so on, are clearly within the definition.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: During the course of time the minister must have had some representation from the municipalities as to how these grants have been working out under the order in council arrangements of previous days. Has any representation been made by the municipalities to allow the ordinary assessment and taxation procedure which is applicable to private enterprise or ordinary ownership in a municipality to apply to government buildings in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: I do not think there has been, because, as I said when this policy was announced, the government would have to reserve to itself the final determination of the valuation. Perhaps I should say that in arriving at that it is the practice of the municipal grants division, which is set up in my department, to have an officer of the division consult with the local assessor, and they discuss the valuation. In some of the larger cities such as Halifax and Ottawa we have retained the services of outside real estate experts to check the valuations and I ;hink I am right in saying that there have oeen no serious differences of opinion with any of the municipalities over the valuations. But the value of government property as carried on most municipal assessment roles was pretty much out of date. No real attention was paid to the properties because they were not paying taxes. Now that we have nearly completed a fairly comprehensive survey I believe we are beginning to get the thing on a fairly even keel. I believe investigations are still going on in some municipalities; for instance, in Halifax there is still some difference of opinion as to certain buildings there. But we are having further checks made. That is the system followed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: In simple terms under this measure, or under the order in council which applied previously, would the dominion government on the average pay as much taxes to a municipality as a similar project or a similar undertaking which was not under government auspices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext:
Making allowance for the four per cent, which is considered a normal proportion of government properties in a municipality, and taking into account that the formula provides for the payment of only 
75 per cent of the balance, I believe it does. The reason 75 per cent was included is that, among other things, it is recognized that in every municipality there is a very considerable amount of tax-exempt property, in addition to government property. It was felt some recognition must be given to the fact that government property and services do bring benefits to the municipalities. That is why 75 per cent of the excess, rather than 100 per cent, was fixed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY
speechtext: I am concerned about the words "in his discretion". How is this discretion to be exercised? If there are principles to guide the minister, I think he should state them to the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES ON CROWN PROPERTY

is common for large industries to negotiate tax agreements with municipalities. Sometimes those are confirmed by legislation. Crown companies have been instructed to follow a similar practice. Harbour boards,
I know, are negotiating with different municipalities now in connection with taxes on their elevators.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one comment that should be


made on the principle of this bill in the light of the discussion yesterday, and the very useful and complete information then submitted to the house by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Benidickson).
The bill, as they have pointed out, follows the pattern of previous bills in relation to C.N.R. financing with the exception of three particulars. The first is the provision of working capital to the extent of $20 million. The second is the authorization to make advance commitments of $111,512,920, and the third is the authorization to use $16,522,000 from reserves for depreciation and debt discount amortization to meet authorized expenditures. One can say, I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that this illustrates the difficulties, when the crown is embarked on a commercial enterprise like the operation of a great railway system, of observing the rules in regard to parliamentary control over finance that we are accustomed to insist upon in the case of financing year by year. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I should like to speak for a few moments on a matter which arose when we were on the orders of the day this morning. I do so because I was astounded at the answer the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave to a question put to him by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry). I was still more startled by the answer he gave to a supplementary question of mine with reference to the same subject.
The hon. member for Rosedale asked the Prime Minister if the government had given or would give consideration to government participation in proposals recently put forward by the Canadian Medical Association, with reference to prepaid medical care. In his answer the Prime Minister indicated that the hon. member for Rosedale had sent him a number of newspaper clippings to make clear the import of the question he asked. The Prime Minister said it was quite clear from those clippings that what was proposed by the medical association was that they should make use of their autonomous powers within the provinces to organize and administer a scheme of prepaid medical care. To my amazement the Prime Minister said that he, as an individual, and other members of the cabinet as individuals were greatly interested in these proposals and welcomed them as further evidence of the concern of the medical profession to increase the efficiency and the scope of their assistance to their fellow Canadians, acting in the role of good Samaritans.
As he went on to answer that question, and indeed in his answer to my question, he made it clear-although I must say in all fairness he was speaking somewhat off the cuff in his answer to my question-that he actually welcomed the idea of a form of health insurance being administered, not by the government but by the medical profession under its own autonomous powers.
I confess this attitude struck me as a case of the Prime Minister's backing away from declared Liberal proposals with regard to health insurance, and I felt it might be well to ask him at that time if consideration would be given at the next session of parliament to the setting up of a special committee to go into this whole question.

The Prime Minister replied to that by repeating the sort of statement he had made to the hon. member for Rosedale, and concluded with these words, which I noted:
I think that it would be a most happy solution if the medical profession would assume the administration of some plan that would be responsible for providing prepaid medical attendance to any Canadian who needed it.
I did not mind the Prime Minister congratulating the medical profession on any evidence of social responsibility that they may give, but I suggest that entirely apart from the views that we in this party hold, the Liberal party is already committed, and has been across the years, to the proposition that if we are going to have a proper program of health insurance it must be administered in the name of all the people by their government.
I just said that the Liberal party has been committed to that principle across the years. I shall go all the way back to 1919. I hold in my hand a copy of the report of the national convention of the Liberal party- this is the convention before the last one- held in Ottawa on August 5, 6 and 7, 1919. I find that the hon. gentleman who was later at that convention elected the leader of the Liberal party was speaking to a lengthy resolution on labour and industrial conditions. There were a number of subdivisions and Mr. Mackenzie King was speaking in support of the propositions set out in that resolution. I quote from page 127 of this official report:
That in so far as may be practicable, having regard for Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces; and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces by effective co-operation between the several governments.
I well remember reminding Mr. King of the support he had given away back in 1919 to the principle of health insurance. In 1948 when Mr. King announced in this house the health grants program which is now in effect -a program only one-fifth of what the federal government proposed to the provinces in 1945-he himself went back and referred to that resolution of 1919 as a piece of unfinished business, something that he and the Liberal party had been committed to since 1919.
I jump across the years to the next Liberal convention, the one held in Ottawa in 1948. I have in my hand two pieces of evidence with respect to that convention. One is a copy of the Ottawa Citizen of Monday, August 9, 1948,
Health Insurance
in which are listed the twenty-one planks of the new platform adopted by the Liberal party at that convention. Plank 11 reads:
A comprehensive social security program.
I have also obtained a copy of the resolutions adopted at that convention in which resolution No. 11 relating to social security is spelled out as follows:
The Liberal party stands for a national program of social security in collaboration with federal and provincial governments with the following objectives: useful employment for all who are willing to work, standards of nutrition and housing adequate to ensure the health of the whole population; social insurance against privation resulting from unemployment, from disability, from ill health and from old age.
The program will include a steady extension of insurance on a contributory basis to protect all citizens from a temporary loss of income and to provide for their old age; health insurance covering medical, dental, surgical and hospital health services on a contributory basis; more equal care and opportunity for all children through family allowances; and pensions for the blind.
It will be noted that there was nothing in that plank adopted at the convention here in Ottawa in 1948 suggesting that the Liberal party would be satisfied with a program of prepaid medical care administered apart from the government by the medical association. The Liberal party reaffirmed the position taken by Mr. King in 1919 calling for a government program of adequate health insurance.
That was the declared policy of the Liberal party, declared in 1919 and reaffirmed in 1948. Its newly elected leader, the present Prime Minister, made a number of speeches during the year that followed the adoption of that new platform. Some of them were collected in the Canadian Liberal, a quarterly publication put out by the Liberal party. I hold in my hand the issue for the fall of 1949 and I And on pages 20, 21 and 22 a report of a national broadcast made on December 16, 1948, by the Prime Minister. From that speech I wish to quote one paragraph:
As for health insurance, the Liberal party has repeatedly said the federal government should help with a sensible and practical nationwide scheme whenever the provincial governments can reach a satisfactory agreement for dominion-provincial co-operation.
It is true that the Liberal party and the government keep talking of this in terms of dominion-provincial co-operation, and with that I agree. However, there is no suggestion anywhere in any literature of the Liberal party that this should be done apart from the government, that it should be administered by the Canadian Medical Association. The position of the Liberal party is clear. It

Health Insurance
believes in health insurance administered by the government, with emphasis upon dominion-provincial co-operation.
I am not taking time to state our C.C.F. position. This house and the country know that we have stood across the years for an over-all social security program, including a comprehensive program of health insurance administered in the name of the people by the government. We were pleased to discover in years gone by that the Liberal party seemed to be moving that way. I recall piling a number of reports up on my desk during another speech earlier this session which indicated the attention that had been given by parliament at the direction of the government to this question of health insurance. But the government seems to be backing away from this whole policy which it has adopted in black and white.
Last year in the special committee on old age security other matters that were not included in our terms of reference came up repeatedly. I think members of that committee will bear me out when I say that it was our feeling that at the earliest possible opportunity there should be established another committee similar to the one we had last year to do a job on this question of health insurance. But this year my questions to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) requesting that such a committee be set up were met with a point-blank "No" on at least two occasions.
Again this morning the Prime Minister simply brushed off my question by expressing satisfaction with the plan proposed by the Canadian Medical Association. I submit that this is an extremely important matter and I think those in this house who should be most concerned about the statement made this morning by the Prime Minister are the members of the Liberal party. The Liberals seem to take the view-

I submit that just as Mr. Mackenzie King was concerned about this matter away back in 1919, just as the Liberal party reaffirmed its position in 1948, it is a matter of such serious consequence that the members of the Liberal party should read the answers which were given this morning and do their best within their own party councils to see to it that their party sticks to its declared policy of health insurance administered not by the medical profession but by the various levels of government in the interests of the people as a whole. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I dealt with this matter the other day in another connection. As far as Canadian government bonds are concerned, of course the government never gave any assurance to any purchaser that he would receive 100 cents on the dollar at any period of time other than maturity. The contract calls for payment of the face value of the bond at maturity and payment of the specified interest in the meantime. In the case of Canada savings bonds, they can be cashed at any time for face value plus accrued interest. Long term government bonds vary according to market conditions. Some of the victory bonds sold at substantial premiums, some as high as 105. At the moment, as I explained the other day, interest rates generally have increased, and the day to day price of government bonds is of course determined by the prevailing interest rate.
I do not know that I can add anything further. The government invests in bonds through various funds such as the unemployment insurance fund; the Bank of Canada invests in government bonds, but they are purchased at prevailing market prices. I repeat that the government never gave any undertaking except that an orderly and stable market would be provided for these bonds.

The government may not
have given an undertaking, but when a great many people bought victory bonds they were given the assurance by those selling them and by the banks in general that they would always be honoured at 100 cents on the dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They will, in accordance with the terms of the bond.

I think they should be so
honoured now.
