speechtext:
No government I know of
issues a long-term obligation with a relatively high interest rate and guarantees the face value at any time. You cannot have absolute security, absolute liquidity and a high interest rate all at the same time.

Surely the minister does
not suggest the government has not given some support to these bonds in order to keep them up to where they have been. It is one thing for the government to say now that they did not give any guarantee the bonds would always sell at par, but the minister will hardly tell the committee that the government has not given some support

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It all depends on what my
hon. friend means by support. The government has been a purchaser and seller of government bonds in line with prevailing interest rates, but it has never attempted to maintain an artificial support for government bonds.
None?
Oh, yes, you did.
There will be wide disagreement with that statement.

I suppose the minister is quite right when he asserts that the government never gave any undertaking that the bonds would always remain at par. It was always understood, of course, that if the bonds were kept to maturity they could be cashed for their face value. But I do not believe that is the whole story, or that the case of the ordinary person who bought these bonds is put in quite the right light. It is quite possible that when people were going around selling the bonds they may have given the assurance that the bond could always be sold at par, though I never heard that assurance given; but we must remember that many of those who bought victory bonds during the war were not people who usually buy and sell bonds of that kind. They were people who really did not know anything about bonds, who perhaps had never had a bond before. They bought these bonds because the government pointed out that it was desirable to save, that it was necessary to do so in order to win that war, and all that sort of thing.
Today the person who bought $100 or $500 worth of these bonds sees those bonds being depreciated on the market. Perhaps that does not make very much difference to him, but in addition those bonds are depreciating every day in their purchasing value as prices rise, so the purchaser is being caught both ways. He is being caught with a bond which is depreciating in market value, and with a bond the money value of which is depreciating so fast that neither interest nor anything of that kind can keep up with it. I really think the government should do something, because it is the little fellow who does not specialize in the buying and selling of these bonds who is taking the rap, as it were. He is being disillusioned as to the stability of the world about him, and his mind is being prepared for any kind of disruptive philosophy that may be put forward. I do not know if the minister or the members of the cabinet

Supply-Finance
understand the harm that is being done to the minds of people because of what is happening today.

I was very much interested in
what the minister had to say about the withdrawal of support on the market. I thought he indicated to the committee that the government or the Bank of Canada, whichever one it is that has been maintaining the support on the market to keep the price of bonds fairly stable at or just about par, withdrew its support. Is it not true that action was taken to withdraw the support about two years ago as a means of establishing a new interest rate, perhaps the first step in a deflationary program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; speaking from memory I think the change in interest rates on government bonds followed the increase in interest rates on long-term government bonds in the United States, which was within the last six or seven months. I remember our last issue of bonds, which was a little less than a year ago, was made at approximately 2f per cent, which reflected nearly the lowest interest rate we had had in the post-war period.
Subsequent to that, as my hon. friend will recall, there was an increase in the longterm interest rate in the United States, following a long wrangle between the treasury and the federal reserve. At or about that time interest rates in Canada on long-term government bonds moved up pretty much in line with the movement and the price which the government of the United States offered for government bonds, and which presumably the Bank of Canada was prepared to pay.
About two years ago, I think it was in the spring of 1949, did not the Bank of Canada announce that it was withdrawing its support?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think what the hon. member has in mind is that about two years ago the Bank of Canada ceased issuing a daily quotation for government bonds.
That is right, and since that time they have gradually withdrawn their support of the daily market?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not be prepared to say that. There is a difference between publishing a daily price which the bank would be prepared to pay for bonds, and simply allowing the normal processes of the market to operate, and the bank purchasing whatever bonds it wished in that market.

Is it not true that the bank did not buy any bonds, at least all the bonds, which were offered to it at certain rates? It runs in my mind that the whole trend has been to allow the price to decline in order

to bolster interest rates generally. That being the case, Mr. Chairman, I am just wondering if the minister and his department have been closing their eyes to this. Not only do people feel that they were guaranteed, in some respects at any rate, one hundred cents on the dollar when they bought those bonds, but they are now coming to realize that if they bought the bonds some years ago they paid dollars that were worth one hundred cents. Those who are forced to sell their bonds now are forced to accept a dollar which will only buy 53 or 54 cents in terms of the dollar of 1935-39. That is a serious thing for bondholders. It is going to make it very difficult for governments to finance the sale of bonds in the future unless something is done to treat the bondholder properly.
It seems to me that that sort of thing is destroying the faith of the people in government. One of two things can be done to restore that faith. The first one is that the government can take steps to restore the value of the Canadian dollar and to stabilize more or less at a uniform level over the years. It seems to me that is one of the responsibilities of government. To put cents back into the Canadian dollar seems to me to be a very important responsibility of government. The second alternative would be to have the Bank of Canada support the price of bonds in the market so that if people need to dispose of their bonds at any time they will be able to get one hundred cents on the dollar. Is that not one of the government's responsibilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must confess that I do not believe, and have never believed, that a government, by governmental action alone, could maintain a stable purchasing power for its unit of currency. Inflation is a most unfortunate phenomenon. I agree with the member for Vancouver East that it is extremely unfortunate that since the end of the war, but really as a result of what happened during the war, we have sustained a substantial measure of inflation. The government is doing what it can or what it believes is possible to check these forces. One of the weapons being used is to permit a mild increase in the interest rates. So far as we are concerned, under the system under which we operate, I do not believe it is possible to control absolutely the internal purchasing power of our unit of currency. We might if we had the Russian system, but without adopting a completely authoritarian system and shutting ourselves off from the rest of the world, I do not believe that is possible.

I wonder if the minister would state whether there is any reason why the holders of these bonds should not be able to

go to a bank and obtain a loan of up to ninety per cent of the face value of the bond? Have any instructions been issued by the government which would militate against obtaining loans of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the government has not issued any instructions to banks in connection with credit. As I explained before, the banks were asked by the Bank of Canada to endeavour to maintain the over-all level of their credit at approximately what it was at the end of the year. They have not been able to achieve that, for reasons which are no doubt good and sufficient. So far as I am aware the banks are prepared to lend on government bonds within proper limits, and I have no doubt they are doing so.

I should like to point out to the minister that a lot of people borrowed money from the banks at that time to buy those bonds. They were encouraged to buy the bond and they borrowed from the bank or anyone at all. They always thought they could get 100 cents on the dollar for them. I do not believe it is fair now when people have to turn in a $100 bond they only get $96. I believe they should be given a 3J per cent bond in exchange for their present bond so they would get 100 cents on the dollar. It is not right for the government to allow the people to take a depreciation on their bonds. I do not think it is good faith or good business.

When these bonds were being sold in 1943 I raised with the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, the question of whether or not these bonds could be guaranteed at par. At that time he stated it was impossible for the government to give that guarantee, but he said it would be the policy of the government to maintain that price as close to par as possible. He also said it was unthinkable -I think those were the words he used-that there should be any very great depreciation so far as the value of these bonds was concerned. I do not suppose the present minister thinks that $2 or $3 depreciation is any very great depreciation. But that depreciation has come about as a direct result of the action of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it has not.
It certainly has.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is completely wrong.

The government has, through the Bank of Canada, instituted a policy of a higher interest rate which has the result of lowering the price or value of these bonds. There is no doubt about that. The minister himself stated that.
Supply-Finance

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Bank of Canada was simply recognizing what had taken place elsewhere.
It was the policy of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be all right for a by-election in Saskatchewan, but it does not mean much to me.

The minister has stated it himself in this chamber. Certainly these bonds were sold to people, and they have depreciated in value. One of the reasons why the minister wants a higher interest rate in this country is to stop inflation. Perhaps by stopping inflation he may in the long run increase the purchasing value of the dollar, and the man who has these bonds may be better off than he would be by selling them at 97, provided the cost of living goes down as a result of this action. But the cost of living has not gone down to date as a result of the action of the government. The cost of living is continuing t- rise; and not only is the man who purchased these bonds losing in the value of the dollar if he cashes them, but he is losing in the value on the bonds themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not unless he sells them.

Certainly not unless he has to sell them. But in many cases if he is to continue to give his family a decent standard of living today, he has got to sell those bonds. Certainly if he wants to purchase any amount of goods or if he wants to extend his business, if he has bonds the only way he can extend his business or the only way he can purchase these goods is, in many cases, by selling those bonds. The people who buy them are certainly guaranteed, as the minister says, one hundred cents on the dollar.
I can remember quite well what happened to these bonds after the first war. They went down to about 85 cents or 87 cents on the dollar. Many of us who had sent home the bit of savings that we had during the war and purchased those bonds came back to Canada and had to sell the bonds for 85 cents on the dollar. The banks or the institutions that purchased them obtained 100 cents on the dollar, and 5 per cent on them as well. To a lesser extent the same thing is taking place right today. I say again that it is the policy of this government, through its action through the Bank of Canada in increasing interest rates, that has depreciated the value of these bonds.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question regarding the effects of their anti-inflationary policy. We all realize that there is a great change in the economic picture in Canada since June of

Supply-Finance
last year. Prior to that time everybody was worried about the possibility of a depression. The Minister of Resources and Development was warning that unless people started to spend their money more freely we were likely to have a depression. He made such a speech before the advertising club in Toronto. The situation is completely different now as a result of the war in Korea. Defence expenditures are competing with private demand for goods. There is a certain amount of what you might call war mentality among the people. They are afraid that goods are going to become scarce so they try to buy in advance in order to make sure that they will get them before they disappear from the market. In addition to that, the kind of talk that is being carried on by several ministers of the government with regard to the fact that we are not having price control today but we may have it in the near future, I think caused many industries to try to jump the gun and raise prices in anticipation that price control might be brought in. I think all that added to the inflationary pressure within the country.
The government's policies today are for the purpose of trying to counteract that inflationary trend. They brought in credit restrictions, and one of the effects has been that car industries are laying off men. I think the minister will agree with me that one thing that we cannot afford today is to have idle men and idle machines. It is bad to have inflation; that is true. But the greatest evil today is idle men and idle machines. The world today needs the greatest production that the countries of the world are capable of carrying out. The minister must admit that the laying off of men in the car industry is a direct result of the government's policy in restricting credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not admit that. I would say that it is a bit of anticipation of demand.
The minister said there was-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When you sell 50,000 units in one month, that is a great many units.
The minister has suggested that there was overproduction; yet I waited three months to get a car. There did not seem to be overproduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You can easily get one now.

Exactly; because the car industries are claiming that as a result of the credit restrictions they cannot sell their cars. They claim that if the restrictions were removed, they would immediately be able to sell them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They may use that as an excuse.
IMr. Quelch.]

Apart altogether from the reason, the point we*must keep in mind is that today we have idle men and idle machines in certain parts of this country. Many people fear that situation will increase. The question is this: What are we going to do about it? I thought that part of the idea behind the government's policy was to try to curtail demand for goods utilizing a large percentage of steel, as steel is needed for war purposes. It seemed to me that perhaps the government had sort of jumped the gun and that they had started to curtail demand before defence expenditures were such as to take up that slack. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that large orders for defence would perhaps be placed with some of these car industries in the near future. But in the meantime these men and these machines are idle. I think that is a point that the minister should be able to give some assurance on. Are we going to see in other industries a repetition of what is happening in the motorcar industry? I am sure the minister will agree that it would be a most deplorable situation if, at a time like this, there continued to be idle men and idle machines. We must have an increase in production. The best way to combat inflation is to expand our production. Can the minister give any assurance that that slack will be taken up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I quite agree with my hon. friend that it is most undesirable that we should have idle men and idle machines. But to take the specific case that he mentions, namely the automobile industry, and as to the lay-off of a week or ten days, or even if it were longer, I am led to believe that there are other fields of endeavour in Canada in which these men could be rapidly utilized.
It is not absolutely essential that we go on, month after month, producing an increasing number of motorcars. There are a great many other things that are needed, and that are not entirely related to defence. For instance, in the month of March almost
50,000	new motor vehicles were delivered through retail channels. By all accounts that was an all-time high, as compared with the same month of last year, when the figure was about 35,000; and that in turn was much higher than the year before. In April the figure was almost 47,000; I have not yet the figures for May. But I believe that motorcars have been turned out rather more rapidly than the community is perhaps able to absorb them. It may need a little bit of averaging for a few months.

But on the general point raised by my hon. friend, we should of course do everything possible to utilize all our men and machines. But the government policy at the moment is intended' to try to utilize the price system to some extent to achieve that redistribution of labour.

I have often wanted to have the minister get into a real fundamental debate on his financial policy. On various occasions since 1945 we have asked the minister to bring forward his estimates early in the session so that we could get down to just such a debate, because there are a great many things that I should like to know and that I am sure that other hon. members would like to find out. However, here we are again on the home-stretch and we are just now getting these estimates before us. I see some hope, however, of getting such a full-dress debate because on the order paper there is a motion-I think it is No. 22 on today's order paper-that in committee of the whole a certain resolution will be moved for the introduction of a measure to consolidate and revise the Department of Finance and Treasury Board Act and so on. I said to some of my colleagues just a few days ago, when I saw this motion on the order paper, that I felt that this would perhaps offer the very finest opportunity for a full-dress debate on the financial policy of this government. Since it is possible that this bill will come forward at some time in the near future, perhaps in the fall session, if not earlier, we think that we should take advantage of it, and I should like to serve notice on the Minister of Finance that that is when we intend to usher in a full-dress debate. We would like him to be prepared and get his armour on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be ready.

I am glad to have him accept, because there are a good many things that we have brought forward over the years, which, while they have not been successfully denied, have not been admitted, and I should like to have some of these things admitted by the government or to have it shown where we are wrong.
However, there is one thing I should like to have the minister do tonight. I wish the minister would take just a few minutes to tell the committee what part the Bank of Canada plays in the formulation of his financial policy. I should like to get clear in my mind just who sets the policy. Is it the Bank of Canada? Is it the treasury? Is it the treasury and the Bank of Canada combined, or what? If the minister would oblige us- I do not ask him for a long detailed exposition-with at least something to help me to
Supply-Finance
get my thinking straight on this whole matter, I should appreciate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The responsibilities of the Bank of Canada of course, as my hon. friend is well aware, are set out in the Bank of Canada Act. It is a corporation which is independent of the government as such. The government owns all the shares of the Bank of Canada and is entitled to the profits, after certain reserves have been established. Under the Bank of Canada Act the governor and the directors of the bank are given specific statutory responsibilities with respect to the issue of currency, and among their responsibilities is to do what is possible within their sphere to maintain the integrity of the currency.
Naturally the governor of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and his permanent officials operate in very close consultation, and the relationships are very close. The Bank of Canada has certain defined statutory responsibilities which, under the statute creating it, it is obliged to carry out. The government has other responsibilities, and among other things I suppose government policy can inevitably affect the value of currency, and to that extent could negative action which the bank might attempt to take. Frankly, I did not come prepared this evening to engage in detailed analysis of the relative relationships between the Bank of Canada and the government. I have not the Bank of Canada Act here, but broadly speaking they are parallel responsibilities. The government, of course, if it were not satisfied with the action taken by the governor and the directors of the Bank of Canada, would have to change the management of the bank.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So that I suppose it is fair to assume that the ultimate responsibility must fall upon the government.

That is the point that I am glad to have. The minister says that he did not come prepared tonight to go into detail with respect to the relative responsibility, and so on, of the treasury and the Bank of Canada. I would like to serve notice on the minister that we would like to go into that in fair detail at a time when it is propitious to do so.
There is one thing further that I should like to have the minister discuss just briefly before the committee. I think he has said on a number of occasions in this committee that he felt the Bank of Canada could quite successfully control the credit policy of the country so as to prevent any undue inflationary effect of the issue of credit. I believe that one of his anti-inflationary measures was

Supply-Finance
to advise the chartered banks, through the Bank of Canada, to begin some curtailment of credit. I think that has been done. The policy is now in effect. I have discussed it briefly with bank managers, and they say that while the order, or the advice, if you want to put it that way, from the Bank of Canada is causing them no end of grief because of necessity for sending to headquarters a great many applications for loans that may extend over let us say twelve months, yet it is working to some extent. If we do grant that the Bank of Canada has some effective control of the amount of credit which the chartered banks can issue, and thus may have some sort of braking effect upon inflationary tendencies, at a time like this, the question that I would like to ask the minister is this: If the reverse situation came about, that is, if we ran into a period where the surpluses of goods in the hands of producers and distributors throughout the country become such as to bring about a threatened period of unemployment and recession, will the minister tell us what mechanism the Bank of Canada has to see that we do not get into a period of disastrous recession or depression.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has asked me what the Bank of Canada should do under these circumstances. As he pointed out, following consultation with the chartered banks, the Bank of Canada felt that economic conditions were such that the chartered banks would be well advised to curtail any further expansion of credit, and I think that by and large the banks are beginning to achieve that end.
They are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If conditions were somewhat
the reverse of what they are today and the deflationary forces were paramount, then I have no doubt that the governor of the Bank of Canada, and the officials of the Bank of Canada as competent technicians in this field, would discuss with the chartered banks and would suggest to them that under these conditions-they would encourage them, shall I put it this way, to pursue a more expansionist policy. These things are all in the exercise of judgment on the part of those who have to make these decisions.

I think that is put very well.
But the minister knows that when surpluses begin to appear and we face possible deflationary conditions confidence is lost very rapidly. It is easy to put a brake on the issue of credit, but does the minister feel that there is a sufficiently strong mechanism closely enough integrated with his own

department's control so that they could prevent a serious loss of confidence and bring things back to a level of economic stability?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer my hon. friend in this way. I think today we have organizations, knowledge and techniques in this field which we did not possess in that unfortunate period from 1930 to 1935 or 1936. We have a central bank. We have a central bank now with considerable experience. We have a central bank with management in which I for one have the greatest confidence; and while, as I say, these questions are all matters of judgment in the use of these weapons, they are pretty blunt weapons. I agree that when deflation sets in deflationary forces are created rather easily, and then confidence is lost. But that is where the exercise of judgment comes in. One must be sure that one does not push either on the contraction side or on the expansion side too strongly.
I hear some of my colleagues condemning me for saying a few words; but this is a very important matter and I think it should be discussed thoroughly.
By you.

I agree with the minister
when he put his curtailment of credit on cars. In the long run I think the majority of Canadians will benefit a lot from it. If this policy of easy credit were to go on those who want to purchase cars now but have only small down payments would have to go to those financial institutions charging 12 or 14 per cent for the balance of the money. The financial institutions would be the ones who would benefit. With the policy of the government today credit controls will be effective until purchasers of cars have enough money for a down payment.
The hon. member for Peace River has raised the matter of municipal financing. It was only this afternoon that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni referred to my municipality of Brokenhead.
Well, I have had some experience along these lines, and I should like to pass on that experience. During my term of office in the municipality which, after ten years, I still have the honour to represent, there were changes in the debt position. When I took office we had a debt of $366,000. After a period of ten years of good financing we do not owe a dollar to anybody.
I notice according to the public accounts that in 1867 at the time of confederation Canada had a national debt of $75,728,641. We operated at a deficit for the first four years. In the fifth year there was a net decrease in public expenditures so that the

national debt was reduced by $503,224. Then for some years we were in the red. But later, in 1881, there was surplus of $1,734,000. They went on for ten years with a deficit every year until the year 1900, when there was a small surplus of $779,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That was under a Liberal
government again.

I am not talking about
Liberals or Conservatives, because I am going to advocate a national policy to reduce Canada's national debt to nil. Then we come down to 1914 when, at the time of the first great war, we had a deficit, and that continued for ten years. After the war was over there was a decrease in the national debt for a period of seven years, which was followed by a period of deficits.
I agree wholeheartedly with the Minister of Finance in the policy he has followed in the last four years. This year while we have very large expenditures to take care of war requirements we are still able to finance those requirements and have money left in the coffers for a reduction in Canada's national debt. I am not saying that it is either good or bad when either of the major political parties is in office; but I do say that with a definite policy for twenty years we would not need to levy one cent more than we are levying right now, with our heavy war expenditures. With an amount of $782 million a year plus interest for a period of twenty years Canada's national debt would be reduced to nothing. I trust the opposition will keep in mind that the surpluses we have had in the last few years, and for which they have criticized the government, are to be used to reduce Canada's national debt, and they have done so to a considerable extent. I would hope that in the next twenty years, whether the Liberal party is in office or not, Canada's national debt would be reduced so that the money we are using to pay interest charges could be used for other social purposes.

I would ask the Minister of Finance whether there has been any change in attitude on his part regarding the effect of financing through the Bank of Canada. He will recall that in the depression years we advocated that the government use the Bank of Canada to finance public works so as to provide employment. That was at a time of large-scale unemployment. The argument his predecessor used, and one which he himself has used, was that if that were done and the money issued reached the chartered banks they would then be in a position to expand their loans ten to one, and thus cause inflation.
Supply-Finance
I notice however that the officials of the Bank of Canada have never agreed with that statement of the minister or his predecessor. They take the stand that just because money was issued would not necessarily mean that the chartered banks would expand their loans ten to one, because all that would be necessary would be for the Bank of Canada to advise the chartered banks that they did not want them to expand their loans, and that in this way it would not be done. In other words, the Bank of Canada believes there is sufficiently close co-operation between themselves and the chartered banks to avoid action of that kind.
I wish to assure the minister than I am not at this time advocating the use of the Bank of Canada, because this is an entirely different situation. But in case that situation does develop, and in case war develops and we find ourselves in a position where, in spite of heavy taxation and heavy borrowing from the people's savings, we still have to have a degree of monetary expansion, as we did in the last war, it might be wise and, in my opinion, would be wise, to use the Bank of Canada rather than the chartered banks. I was wondering if the minister would agree that in that case there is a sufficiently close co-operation between the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks to assure that if we did finance to a certain extent through the Bank of Canada rather than through the chartered banks it could be done without expanding the amount of money issued by ten to one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to commit myself to agreeing completely with the hon. member on the point. As he has indicated, I have had occasion to discuss it at another time. It is a complex and technical matter. The relationship between the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks might be very close; but if the expanded currency credit by the Bank of Canada were to get into the hands of the chartered banks and could not be used by them I would think it would be extremely difficult to prevent their expanding in approximately the ratio he has suggested. However, I do not think it is wise to be too dogmatic in these matters. If a condition such as he suggests were to develop again I have no doubt that, as was the case in 1939, some moderate expansion might not only be necessary but might well be desirable.
Through the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it was done that way.

I believe my observations might apply to either item 112 or 113. On more than one occasion the minister has made a good deal of the government's efforts,

Supply-Finance
so called, to reduce expenditures. One would have expected that, with that policy originating in the Department of Finance, there would have been reductions in the expenditures of that department, and that it would have led the way. I notice that the two items under the heading of general administration total this year $13,590,710, whereas last year they were only $12,758,245, or an increase of $832,465. I realize, of course, there has been an increase in salaries paid to civil servants, and those increases were accepted by all members as timely and well warranted. But I was wondering why we do not find in the estimates of this department any perceptible decrease in expenditure.
We listened with interest to the observations of the hon. member for Springfield, and recalled what had been said on many occasions by the Minister of Finance about the fruits of the policy of high surpluses, even if not budgeted for, and debt retirement. But when we come to examine the public debt charges at page 17 we find that the charges being provided for this year actually show an increase over last year. Last year the total was $423,710,000 and this year they have risen to $427,363,000. I am quite sure that the increase in the interest rate on government borrowings, which has been evident in the past six months, is not reflected as yet in these estimates and there must be some further explanation for the increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The increase in the general administrative item, as in the earlier items, is due entirely to increased salaries. In the case of the general administration vote we have 51 positions less than last year. Notwithstanding that reduction in staff, our payroll will be $50,000 higher. In the case of the comptroller, which of course is a very large establishment, we have 275 positions less than last year, or 3,897 positions as against 4,172. The increase in that branch is almost entirely due to general salary revisions together with the increased cost of office supplies and equipment, new cheque writing equipment and additional mailing charges in respect to larger volume of family allowances cheques.
In the case of charges for interest on the public debt, the increase there is due entirely to involuntary borrowings. By involuntary borrowings I mean payments made into our pension fund, and into the annuities account. When we sell annuities we have to pay three per cent, or credit three per cent interest to the account. Then there is also the interest on Canada savings bonds. The increase in that item is due entirely to this form of involuntary borrowing.

Even taking into account these forms of involuntary borrowings, we
EMr. Fleming.]	[DOT]
must remember that the debt was lower at the end of 1950 than it was at the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This does not show as part of the funded debt.
Even taking account of the surplus that the minister has mentioned and which we were given to understand went entirely for debt reduction-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Net debt reduction.
I think most members of the house understood that it was in fact a net debt reduction. Are we to understand that because of these involuntary borrowings there was no net debt reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know my hon. friend appreciates the difference between gross and net debt. While on the one side of the balance sheet, in the case of these pension funds, and so on, we have an obligation which is part of our gross debt; in the net debt we take credit for the asset which is the amount in the fund.

I should like to refer to the FAO for a moment and I know it may be said that this is part of the Department of Agriculture or the Department of External Affairs. The matter I wish to deal with has to do with the financing of exports of commodities. Two days ago I quoted from the report of the director general of FAO for 1949-50 where he referred to the fact that there is far too little food for the world's hungry mouths and that an increase in production would not be enough to keep pace with the number of human beings. Then he went on to say that more and more people realized that such conditions were no longer necessary.
I think the food and agriculture organization has done some fine work in the past but unfortunately much of that work has been nullified by the member nations turning down its recommendations. That same report refers to the fact that two or three proposals were made to deal with the distribution of surplus food to the hungry people of the world, and I quote from page 13 of the report as follows:
The first proposal for a world food board which would buy supplies during periods of surplus and release them during periods of scarcity, was turned down by governments.
The next proposal of the FAO was for an international commodity clearing house, with much narrowed functions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Item 96 deals with the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations. I am afraid I am not prepared to discuss this matter under my estimates.

I am simply giving a background for the question I am going to ask

which I think comes directly within the minister's sphere. As I mentioned, the international commodity clearing house was turned down. Here is an interesting point. Canada's delegate to the food and agriculture conference, the Minister of Agriculture, took the stand that there was nothing in the international commodity clearing house that could not be done individually by a nation. That was one argument he presented for turning down that proposal.
We may soon face a situation where we have surpluses of food in Canada and there will be certain countries in the world where people are starving but where they will be unable to finance imports of our food. The Minister of Agriculture said that there was nothing in the idea of an international commodity clearing house that we could not do by ourselves. The conditions out west never looked better. I do not want to be too optimistic because as a farmer I know how conditions can change, but there is more moisture this year than we have had for many years.
If we have large crops with resultant surpluses, if we are faced with the fact that people are starving in a country like India and India is unable to pay for our surplus food, will the minister give us the assurance that his department will provide the means by which exports of food to needy countries can be financed? I have great confidence in the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but after all his job is to trade our food for the products of other countries. If a country has no commodities to trade with us the Minister of Trade and Commerce will not be able to trade with them.
The responsibility will then lie with the Minister of Finance to find ways and means of getting the surplus food of this country to the nations that need it. Mind you, our delegate turned down the recommendation for an international commodity clearing house which would have provided the means by which that surplus food could have been delivered to needy people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid that I am not familiar with the proceedings of FAO and what methods are adopted to finance foreign trade at some future time. I do not think it would be appropriate for me to give an assurance now as to what we would do. That would be a matter of policy that would have to be decided at that time. We were discussing export credits a little earlier, and by means of loans to the United Kingdom and other countries we have assured a fairly steady market for our export products. I would not attempt this evening to forecast
Supply-Finance
what the policy of the government would be under some future set of conditions.

If in the future we have a surplus of food and if there are people in any part of the world needing that food, all I want the minister to do is to assure us that his department will see that ways and means are found by which that food can be got to those hungry people. In other words, we want assurance from the minister that his department will not allow food to rot while there are hungry people in any part of the world needing that food. I am not asking the minister to declare what his policy will be; I am just asking for that assurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the ten or eleven years I have been a member of this house there has been no case in which food has rotted because we have been unable to find a means of disposing of it to people who needed it, and I hope I will not have that experience during such time as I remain here.

That may be true about Canada, but food has been allowed to rot in the United States. They had a great many surpluses which were stored; eggs, for example, were kept for so long that they rotted, and today they are giving food away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have enough troubles of my own without looking after any in the United States.
Just as a point of interest I may tell the minister that fish was dumped in Newfoundland last year.
Under what item does the Canadian farm loan board come?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told there is no item covering it. That is a separate corporation, as my hon. friend knows, and there is no vote for it. If my hon. friend wanted some information I would be glad to have him ask for it now on the general item.

It is not exactly information; I want to make a suggestion to the minister. The Canadian Farm Loan Board Act was passed in 1929, and under it loans were made on farm lands of up to 50 per cent of the appraised value of the land. The total amount of the loan that could be made to any one borrower was $5,000. In 1934 the act was amended to permit a second mortgage loan of up to $2,000. Since that time there has been no change in the amount that can be loaned, and today we find that these amounts are not large enough. The value of land, of machinery and of everything the farmer has to buy today has doubled or tripled since 1929, and many young farmers find it

Supply-Finance
impossible to obtain an economic farm unit with the amount of money that can be borrowed under this act.
Until 1945 these loans carried interest at the rate of 5 per cent on first mortgages and 5J per cent on second mortgages. At that time the interest rate was reduced to 4J per cent on first mortgages and 5 per cent on second mortgages. The difficulty today, as I am sure the minister will realize, is that the amount that can be borrowed is really too small to obtain enough land. The cost of land is greater, and all the expenses that go into the establishment of an economic unit for farming are easily twice today what they were when this act came into force. If this legislation is to do the job it should do I believe the maximum amount that may be borrowed must be increased.
There is a demand for these loans. The 1950 report states that the board carried forward 565 loan applications not disposed of during the previous fiscal year, and received a further 4,639 applications. It states further that the loans granted amounted to $5,189,400 as compared with $4,919,300 the previous year. So there is a demand for this type of loan. The purpose would be served much better, I believe, if the minister could see his way clear to have the amount of the loan that can be made to one applicant increased to at least $10,000 instead of $5,000, because today $10,000 will not do any more than $5,000 did when the act was passed in 1929. I just want to bring this to the attention of the minister and ask him to consider it-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be glad to do that.
-and see if something cannot be done to increase the amount of these loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be glad to take these representations into consideration.

I would like to ask the minister one or two questions before the item carries. I gathered when the minister replied to the hon. member for Peace River that he intimated, if he did not state, that one of the functions of the Bank of Canada was to guarantee the integrity of the Canadian currency. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I put it in just those terms. I do not remember exactly what I said, but what I intended to say was that one of its functions was to see to the management of the Canadian currency, that it should be issued in proper form, not to excess, and so on.

I would like to know whether the minister would agree that the

expression "integrity of the Canadian currency" would be accurate. Would he accept that as being an expression of the concept that is in his mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether or not I used that term. I think perhaps that word might be just a little too strong. There is a limit to what the bank can do. I gave a fairly carefully worded offhand explanation and pointed out that whatever the bank might do or whatever it felt it might do could be negatived by government policy, and that therefore in all these matters the ultimate responsibility would have to fall on the government. I really do not think I can elaborate on that very much tonight.
I would like very much to have the minister tie himself down to a definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He never ties himself down.

I am quite sure of that. He dashes along very cavalierly and never commits himself to anything. Now let him commit himself. Would he accept the expression "the integrity of the Canadian currency"? A moment ago he said that currency would not be issued to excess. What does he mean by that? I want something we can get our teeth into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry; would the hon. member repeat his question. I was checking on something with my experts.

I would like the minister to check with his experts, the very best he has, because he will need them. I want to know whether the expression "integrity of the Canadian currency" would be the one the minister would choose rather than "soundness of the currency".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would prefer "integrity".
So do I. Then would you just tell us what you mean by integrity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the Oxford dictionary here, but I would be prepared to accept the definition it contains.

The minister has his
experts there; they must have an Oxford dictionary. How would his experts define the integrity of the Canadian currency?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that that is their responsibility. I will have to assume responsibility for what is meant by that.
Then let the minister take the responsibility right now and tell us the meaning of that phrase as applied to Canadian currency.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman, and it is not likely to be carried tor quite a while. We want something we can get our teeth into. One of the biggest troubles when many people talk about money is that they are just not careful about the words they use. If we can get some words we can actually rely upon we can use them as a base from which to begin. Would the expression "integrity of currency" be one that could be substituted for "soundness of currency"? In the days of R. B. Bennett we had a tremendous amount of talk about sound money, and Mr. Dunning carried on the expression, sound money. What does sound money really mean?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No. I would like the minister to answer that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As Mr. Bennett would have said, I think sound money means sound money.
I wonder if the minister could not improve upon that definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I doubt it. I do not believe I could.

Then would the minister say a sound dollar is one that retains a constant purchasing power for a given length of time, so that a dollar in 1949 would buy practically the same amount of wheat or any other commodity as a dollar in 1939? Would that be a definition of "sound" that we could accept?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly that would be the counsel of perfection; it would be a splendid thing if money retained a constant purchasing power, but in this imperfect world unfortunately it does not.

We could more appropriately say under this exceedingly imperfect financial system under which we work it is almost impossible to obtain. The minister evidently agrees that a sound dollar is a dollar that retains its purchasing power at about the same level over a period of years. I believe the minister will grant that since 1939 the Canadian dollar has been exceedingly unsound.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say that.
You would not say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Let us examine that
matter for a moment or two. The soundness of a dollar is to be determined by the price of goods, is it not? If the price of goods doubles, the value of the dollar is halved. In other words, a dollar is by no means sound which does not maintain its purchasing power. Now, the price of goods in Canada
Supply-Finance
has not quite doubled in these ten years but it has come very close to it. The Canadian dollar failed completely to remain sound. Would the minister challenge that statement?

That is quite right, but
there is still time. We are still young.
