I do not believe the minister would care to say that the Canadian dollar remained sound during that period. Its value has been steadily falling. The minister will say, "Well, that is the result of inflation." Will the minister tell us exactly what inflation is, the way he uses the word?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that at this late hour of the evening I should attempt to embark

Supply-Finance
on that subject. I shall use the short definition, although it is an oversimplification. It is a case of too many dollars chasing too few goods.

The minister says it is too many dollars chasing too few goods. Let us examine this thing with a little care. In April of 1946 the price of steel advanced $5 a ton in Canada, I presume as a result of a request of the three steel companies and with the consent of the Canadian government. Will the minister show how the amount of money then in circulation had anything to do with that increase in the price of steel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not my department, Mr. Chairman.

It is very vital to the question under discussion. According to the minister's definition that increase in the price of steel ought to have been the result of a surplus of money in circulation. It was nothing of the kind. That advance of $5 in 1946 was manipulated apparently or demanded by the steel companies and permitted by the government. The money in circulation had nothing to do with it at all.
During the year 1946 the steel workers struck. As a result of that long strike of about eighty-two days they obtained an advance in wages. The advance in wages increased the cost of the production of steel and everything else all over the country, because the people all over the country began demanding comparable increases in wages. Those increases in wages forced up the cost of production and forced up the prices of commodities. Will the minister show how the money in circulation had anything to do with those advances in prices? Will he show how too many dollars chasing too few goods had anything to do with that increase in price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought everyone knew that there was not enough steel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know that my hon. friend does not want to delay unduly the passage of these estimates. I hope that he will not feel that he should engage in a long discussion as to freight rates at this hour in the evening and at this stage in the
Supply-Finance
session. We have had quite an extended discussion on inflation and its causes, both on the budget and at other times. I would appeal for his co-operation and for the co-operation of other members of the committee, in seeing that we try to stick as closely as we can to the item under discussion. We have had well over an hour of discussion now under the item of departmental administration. I am not attempting to curtail that discussion, but I would hope that we might try to keep it as closely as possible to the item that is before us.

I sympathize deeply with the minister, because the minister is in the awkward and untenable position of attempting to defend an utterly indefensible financial system. That is just exactly where his trouble lies. It is not his fault. It is the fault of the financial system under which he is attempting to act. As to delaying the estimates, I will tell you what I will do. I have been waiting for a long time to get a talk with the minister, and the opportunity has finally come. I am sure he has also been waiting a long time to get a talk with me. The opportunity has now come. I am right here, and I am going to stay right here so he can get at me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not want to get at my hon. friend. I think too highly of him for that.

I will agree with the minister to allow his other items to go through, if he will hold this one and let it stand so that we may finish up this discussion in a workmanlike fashion some time a little bit later on. I would be quite willing to do that, or I will continue now what we are at present discussing, namely this item of inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, we are discussing an item of $1,500,000 for departmental administration.

Oh, yes; but under departmental administration is included everything pertaining to the minister's department. Certainly one of the minister's responsibilities has to do with the price structure, the control of inflation, the maintenance of the "integrity" of the Canadian dollar or the "soundness" of the Canadian dollar, or any other less objectionable or more accurate word the minister can find.
Out of this amount the minister pays his advisers for bad advice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is within his rights. I appeal to him, however. As I say, we have discussed this question for eleven years now. But in those eleven or almost

Supply-Finance
eleven years I have never succeeded in completely convincing my hon. friend; and he has never succeeded in convincing me that the financial system is wrong. He may be able to do it tonight, but I would doubt it.

What I am trying to do tonight is to find out whether the minister can laugh off or explain away irrefutable facts; and what I am giving him now are irrefutable facts pertaining to the so-called "inflation", the rise in prices. The matter is fundamental and it is exceedingly serious because as long as we go forward cavalierly, in the face of facts, saying that this increase in prices is a result of too many dollars chasing too few goods, we shall in the next few years make the most ghastly economic blunders that it is conceivable for a government to make. But if we face the fact that this increase in prices is not a result of a scarcity of goods but is a result of deliberate manipulation upwards, of deliberate profiteering; and if we grant that, then we shall adopt an entirely different method of dealing with the matter of high prices.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to hold up these estimates. I have a happy home to go to and a lovely province to live in. I should like to get back there. But I also have a job to do here, and it is vital to the interests and the welfare of Canada, that I do my job so far as I can see. If the minister feels that he would rather have all this out on item one, we will have it out on item one; because I think I am strong enough- -to last until eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure of that.

I should like to- go on one step further. I could give a number of other details- that I have here a-s to the increase in the cost of clothing which occurred this very year. I have letters right here from Lethbridge people about the advances that were made by the wholesale companies to the retail companies. No mention is made of too many dollars chasing too few goods. In every single letter the company concerned says: Our costs have increased until we cannot stand, it any more and we have raised the price. Then we have the absolute hypocrisy -and that is the only word you can use-of the Department of Finance, the bank managers and all the financial people of that kind all over this country, in trying to delude the people of Canada into believing that the present increase in price is and has been the result of too many dollars chasing too few goods! That is one of the most consummate falsehoods ever perpetrated on a people.
Let us face facts just exactly as they are. Let us take the last rise in prices, namely,

the one in wood pulp. Can anyone possibly show how that increase in the price of wood pulp for paper was the result of too many dollars chasing too few rolls of paper? Well, what utter nonsense! The Minister of Trade and Commerce stood up in his place the other day and explained the increase in that price. I thought he made out a pretty good case. He went on to show that the costs of these pulp companies had increased so much that, although they had heroically absorbed a number of these costs, the time had come when they simply had to have an increase in the price of their wood pulp and paper. I imagine that every hon. member in the committee tonight heard him do that and will testify to what I say. That is the last one I have.
What is going to be the result of this increase in the paper price? It is going to cause an increase in costs all across the board. All we need is just two or three more increases like that in major -commodities in Canada and we shall have an irresistible demand on the part of labour for an increase in wages, just as we had an irresistible demand last year for an increase in wages on the railroads. We realized it was irresistible and we yielded. Can anyone say that the cause of the increase in railroad freight rates is the fact that we have too many dollars chasing too few railroad cars, or too few engines? What utter nonsense!
The minister has left the committee.
He could not take it.

He could not take the
facts. To me a fact is simply this-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The minister has been sitting here seven hours today and I think he is entitled to go out and stretch his legs.

I am glad the parliamentary assistant said that. I myself have been here seven hours today. I realize the minister has the right to go out and stretch his legs. It is well to be known that he is not here, while these important questions are being asked.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member could go
out and in during the seven hours, but the minister has been piloting bills and his estimates throughout the entire sittings of this house this morning and afternoon and evening. I think it is most unfair to suggest that the minister went out simply because he was upset by the remarks of the hon. member. He has been listening most intently all through to the comments of the hon. member.

While the minister is out
stretching his legs, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the assistant to the minister would not mind answering a question or two. Since his advisers are sitting in front of him it is quite likely that he can answer the questions just as effectively as the minister himself. I should like to ask this question. Assume that the minister is right in his answer-I am not saying he is, because the hon. member for Lethbridge says he is not-that there are too many dollars chasing too few goods. Does the minister absolve himself from all responsibility for the expansion of credit that has taken place throughout the last number of years? For instance, toward the end of the war there was a loan floated by the government. Bond salesmen were out to raise this loan. Of course it was raised. They tagged the office girl; they tagged the man in the factory; and they said, you can even buy bonds on the instalment plan. What happened? The minister floated that loan. He permitted people who wanted to buy bonds to go to the bank and borrow money to buy those bonds. The banks encouraged them to buy through them, and when the bond purchaser went to the bank to borrow the money for bonds, new money was issued. The minister knows that. If new money was issued, then new money was put into circulation, when goods should have been coming off the assembly line, if there was a deficiency of goods.
That was his plan; that was the government's financial policy, and I wish hon. members would recognize this. I notice that when questions are asked sometimes and there is persistence used in attempting to extract an answer from the minister, there is some levity in some quarters. The minister himself rises and says: "Well, the hon. member for Lethbridge and I have been talking about this for the last eleven years, and we do not understand each other." That does not answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That	was not what I said.
I said, neither of us had been able to convince the other.

I see. Well, I did not
scrutinize the answer so carefully but that does not change my point. Simply because they are not able to understand each other does not answer the question. I am asking a definite question on the basis that the minister believes at least that his answer was right in respect to too many dollars chasing too few goods. Does he absolve himself in that?
What I was going to say to hon. members is this. A certain levity exists because hon.
Supply-Finance
members take the present financial system for granted, and assume that there is nothing wrong with it; that the government only errs in too much taxation or too little taxation, or taxing here instead of taxing there. But that is not the thing that is basically or particularly wrong. That is the boil that breaks out on the back of the neck. It wouldn't matter if it broke out somewhere else. If the blood is wrong in the system then you cannot cure the boils. The fact of the matter is that there are certain basic and fundamental things that are wrong with the financial system followed by the government. One thing that is wrong is-hon. members do not recognize this. I am certain that the evidence is there and the minister knows it. When the minister goes to the bank to borrow freshly created money which is lent at an interest, that freshly created money cannot be paid back without interest being created too. That is only a remark in passing.
Hon. members assume there is nothing wrong. Hon. members assume that when banks lend money they lend their depositors' money. They do not. The minister knows that they lend freshly created money which they themselves create with a stroke of a pen in their books. The minister knows that.
I am asking him whether he absolves himself from all responsibility when he knew that goods were in short supply? He himself admits that he encouraged the expansion of money in this country. You have to fix the blame somewhere. It is all right to say: Well, there is too much money chasing too few goods. Who is responsible for too much money? It does not drop down from heaven; it does not grow on trees. Somebody gave instructions to expand the credit of the country just as the minister gives instructions to restrict credit expansion. They cannot tell us there is too much money chasing automobiles. For the last day or two we have read in the newspapers that some of the factories are going to close down because there are too many cars.
I would like to focus the blame. Who is responsible? Does the minister absolve himself from all responsibility in not being able to manage the financial affairs of the country and to restrict credit at the proper time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am a modest man and never try to absolve myself from responsibility. I am prepared to take my share of responsibility for such things as I, as Minister of Finance, have done in matters of financial policy during the five years I have been Minister of Finance. But I like to believe it

Supply-Finance
has -been pretty sound financial policy, and I am quite prepared to stand on the record of it.
We will have to accept the minister's answer, but I certainly expected cne with a little more strength to it than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a little late in the
evening.

Is it a sound financial policy when people with money in the bank ten years ago find that today that money is worth only half what it was worth then? If the minister will call that a satisfactory policy, then I will eat my hat, right here in the middle of the chamber of the House of Commons.

Now that the hon. member for Macleod has joined me in the argument, and I appreciate very much that he has, I should like to focus attention of the committee on the two points I was making.
The first of these was the point on which the hon. member for Macleod closed his speech, namely that the Canadian dollar has not been kept sound.
Nor wholesome.

And if the Canadian
dollar has not been kept sound we certainly cannot say that the Canadian financial system, which is based upon that dollar, has been kept sound.

Fixed assets have doubled,
though.
Probably; but that is not money.

There are four times as many
dollars.

But the dollars are worth only about half. Let us keep our eye on the ball-and the ball in this case is the dollar. I maintain that the government has not a policy whereby it can keep the dollar sound. In the depression the dollar was appreciated until it was worth about twice what it was worth in 1927, so that people who contracted debts in 1927 had to pay the full amount of the debts plus interest in dollars that were twice as hard to get as in 1927. This brought about an almost inconceivable destruction of wealth and well-being in the country.
Then, a few years after that, the value of the dollar went down, so that those who had saved a little money have had it stolen from them in the last five years.
The same system both times.

The next question was
one of inflation, and I wish to concentrate on it again. The hon. member for Macleod

said he was not assuming that there are too many dollars chasing too few goods. I am not, either. When we closed the war in 1946, let it be borne in mind that our productive capacity was geared to the conduct of a war. We had 1,250,000 of our finest producers in the war. Some 750,000 of them were overseas fighting, and the rest of them were in war plants. All those people came out of the war and entered the productive forces of the country.
Are we to be told that, with all that additional productive capacity to be applied to the production of consumer goods, we could not produce enough goods? What nonsense! If we could produce enough goods in 1946 for the demands of this country, then there must be something radically wrong with our financial and economic system if we cannot produce enough now. The men came back from war. We stopped producing munitions of war. No longer did we operate in the activities of war, but rather concentrated on our domestic economy. In the name of common sense, if we did not produce enough to keep up with the dollars seeking goods, then whose fault was it, and how in the world did it come about?

Working twelve hours a day,
seventy-two hours a week.

We were working plenty
of hours in 1946 to produce all the goods we needed in Canada. And just in a little while I will show plenty of evidence of a surplus of goods.
Only the other day we had the Minister of Trade and Commerce making a very positive statement. Perhaps I should read it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Dispense.

No; we do not like to be told these things! But I am telling you that we are getting at the facts and we are getting some truths, and from someone who knows. That is a sufficient answer-and he is telling someone who apparently does not know. Maybe that is a sufficient answer.
I am quoting from good authorities recognized in this country. In this connection I would refer to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on June 14, where he says:
There is another important element in the defence production program, and that is manpower. We have a tight manpower situation. As civilian producers, with exceptionally heavy stocks, run into consumer resistance, they may find it necessary to cut back staff.
Did the Minister of Trade and Commerce know what he was talking about when he spoke about exceptionally heavy stocks in the hands of civilian producers, or did he not?
No one in Canada did.

I am assuming the minister did know. He goes on to say:
I am satisfied, however, that such personnel will be absorbed quickly into defence or defencesupporting industries. There will be minor dislocations, but I am satisfied that there is sufficient labour of the right kind in Canada to support our defence program as well as a flourishing civilian economy.
What does "flourishing civilian economy" mean? Is that one in which there are not enough shoes being produced, enough stockings, enough bread and butter, enough fish, or one in which all those things and other goods are being produced in abundance? It can only mean that we are producing in abundance, and that we have already in store an abundance.
The only reason that that abundance has not been manifested in the market is that the people processing it are fearful they will break the market and bring down the price of these goods to a ruinous level. That is all. They are deliberately holding their goods of! the market.
I should like now to turn to one other aspect of this whole matter of the responsibilities of the Department of Finance. I am sorry the minister is not in his seat, but I am glad he has the opportunity to go out to stretch his legs. However, the parliamentary assistant is a very promising young man, and his answers ought to be just as acceptable as those of the minister.
It is recognized I believe that if you are going to have your dollar completely sound, you must have enough dollars in your economy and they must be circulated in the right places. You must not have too many, and you must have enough.
When did the average Canadian people have more?
I do not believe they have had more. I agree with the hon. member.
You have made another convert.

He is simply a man who faces facts. He has not been carried down the primrose path by the minister, that is all. We have much more money in circulation now than we had in 1939 or 1945, yet we have not more than enough to consume the goods which are in store if the goods were made available.
You have plenty, haven't you?

We have plenty, that is all right. I am quite interested in the hon. member's questions. I do not want to repress any question just as long as it is honest. This is a most important matter. A few minutes
Supply-Finance
ago the hon. member for Peace River asked the minister if the Bank of Canada had any mechanism whereby it could increase the number of dollars in circulation if it should be found that there were too few dollars chasing too many goods, which was exactly the thing that happened in the depression.
Just as soon as you have too few dollars chasing too many goods you have a fall in price, there is an increase in unemployment and you have a depression. Up to the present time under the present financial system the only means that mankind has discovered to get a nation out of a depression is to go to war. That is the only means that has been used up to the present time to get people out of depressions.
Oh, oh.
Name a time when they did not.

There was 1914. We do not want to go too far on that. I repeat that the only way you can get people out of a depression is to increase the money in circulation as you increase it through war. If the minister had been here I wanted to ask him a question. I do not know whether I win ask the parliamentary assistant, or whether I will just answer the question. Suppose that the Bank of Canada was being managed by the two gentlemen who now sit in front of the parliamentary assistant and who I think are pretty high in the confidence of the Bank of Canada. Suppose that we found in Canada that there were too many shoes, too many clothes of all kinds and too many hats. Would they advise the chartered banks to lend money to anybody who wanted to produce more shoes or more clothing or more hats? Would they? Not by any manner of means.
That was exactly the trouble in 1931, 1932 and 1933. All hon. members of this house can remember how in those days it was said that we had overproduction. The result was that no bank in the country dared lend to produce anything because there was already in the economy of Canada more of everything than could be bought by the people. Will the experts who sit in front of the parliamentary assistant tell us how in the world the Bank of Canada by means of an "expansionist" policy could cause the banks to lend money and get it into circulation when they dared not lend money because of overproduction? There will be no answer because the Bank of Canada has no answer. The Minister of Finance has no answer.
The present financial system has no answer. The question is just not answerable under the present system.
Suppose the Bank of Canada, realizing that say one billion dollars more of purchasing

Supply-Finance
power had to go out into circulation in order to have enough dollars chasing the goods there were, how would the Bank of Canada proceed to get those dollars out into circulation?
That was the question I asked the minister.
That is what the hon. member for Peace River asked.
Carried.

I know you would like to have it carried because the pressure is getting worse all the time. You are getting into difficulties deeper and deeper. Of course you would like to have it carried, but it is not going to carry until some of these questions are answered. Last December the best informed producers in Canada were worrying for fear there would be a depression. What we want to understand is what will be done if a depression comes on? A depression will come on just as soon as you have more goods in circulation than you have dollars to chase them.
Who will be the judge?

I should like to quote from a press dispatch which has an important bearing on this matter. The Lethbridge Herald contained a Canadian Press report of December 4 from Montreal headed, "Sees recession soon unless war grows worse." This reads:
Alexander Gray, Sr., Toronto industrialist, Friday night predicted "a definite recession within twelve months if the war situation . . . does not grow worse."
There are a lot of people who are almost afraid we are going to have peace in Korea, that we are not going to be able to use all these war munitions.
I hope you are right for once.

There are a lot of people who are wishing that down underneath because they realize that if we do not go to war we are going to be plunged into a depression and under the present financial system they would not know what to do.
Who are those people?

The article continues:
Mr. Gray, president of Gray-Bonney Tool Company Limited, and a director of the Canadian Exporters' Association, addressing the Society of Automotive Engineers, added:
"This boom is built on uncertainty, on fear of the unknown, on credit. When you read of what our government is going to do, and what the United States government is going to do, it changes from week to week, from month, to month. News of probable defence orders is announced months before actual orders are placed.
When you talk to business executives they throw up their hands. Their plants are running to capacity."

I do not think I need go on any longer with that particular article because that is sufficient to establish my point. Let us suppose that we increase our productive capacity in Canada fast enough to supply all the needs of the men overseas and more goods than all Canadians need. Can the Bank of Canada suggest a single means whereby adequate money could be put into circulation? No, it cannot. That is what raises the whole question of the Social Credit contention concerning debt-free money. I would like to ask the parliamentary assistant a question, but first let me say what happened. As most hon. members know, in 1916-17, during the war, under the Finance Act of 1914 the dominion government issued and spent into circulation $26 million. It was debt free. No bank printed it; the treasury did, and the government spent it. Would the parliamentary assistant say one of those twenty-six million dollars was a sound dollar?
It contaminated all the rest of the dollars.
Carried.

Of course the parliamentary assistant dare not give the answer. The answer would have to be that it was. A sound dollar is a dollar that has stable purchasing power. In other words it has enough goods at stable prices behind it for it to chase and not too many. This $26 million was issued and spent by the government of the time. Will anyone dare say-I know the parliamentary assistant will not-that one of those dollars was unsound? It would have exactly the same purchasing power as the dollars already in circulation, dollars that had been loaned there. Very well. The soundness of a dollar depends upon the goods and services available for it to chase and upon the price structure. There is no answer to that; that must be a sound dollar. In other words the soundness of a dollar must depend upon the amount of goods in the community and the price structure. If the debt free dollar spent into circulation does not cause prices to increase, then that dollar is just as sound as though it had been loaned by a bank. There can be no other conclusion. The minister has come in now; I would ask him that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am going to say to my hon. friend that I think it is an imposition upon the members of the committee that one member should take up the time he has taken today in constant repetition. He made a forty minute speech this morning on gold which was out of order on the housing bill. Since nine o'clock this evening he has been

talking almost incessantly, and I think it is an imposition upon the other members of the committee.
Hear, hear.

May I just say to the minister in reply that if he and his parliamentary assistant would show some disposition to answer the questions which have been asked probably we would be through in half the time.
Or some ability to do so.
It is coming [DOT] to a pretty pass when an hon. member has to work as hard as the hon. member for Lethbridge has worked to try to get answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He has had his question
answered a dozen times, and I do not intend to answer it again this evening.

The discussion that has taken place has been absolutely fundamental to the financial policy of this country, which is before the committee in the first item of the minister's estimates. For months we have been trying to get him to face this situation. We have told him for the last three years that I know of that we were going to force him into a position some time where he would have to answer these questions, where he would have to defend his policy. It is no defence to just sit there and give a general brush-off, and drag red herrings across the trail; nor is it a defence to protest to you, Mr. Chairman, against a person taking time. What are we here for but to take time to get satisfactory answers to the questions the people of Canada want answered? I like my hon. friend; I have always admired him, but I have warned him time and again that this was coming and he should have been ready. He is not ready, as he said tonight; and it is high time he was ready.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say any such thing. I answered questions for an hour, and I have answered about all I can answer this evening.

The people of this country will be able to judge the style of those answers. They will be able to judge whether or not the minister has the information. When they look over the record of the debate this evening they will say the Minister of Finance did not know anything, he did not answer anything. From the answers that have been put on the record tonight the people of this country who read this debate will say the Minister of Finance did not answer a single question. He tried to brush us off. To begin with tonight I tried to get the minister to delve into these things and give us something like a reasonable answer. I told him we were looking forward to the time when a certain
Supply-Finance
resolution now on the order paper would be called, and I said at that time we hoped to launch a full-dress debate on the government's financial policy. But in order to get some information I thought I would like to have, I asked some questions. That was followed by questions from other members of the group.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mostly by one member.

I think the hon. member for Lethbridge tried valiantly to get answers to the questions. He was not given satisfaction in a single one, as the record will show. He is entitled to satisfactory answers to those questions, and so is the country. As far as I am concerned, since the minister is taking the position he is, I am not going to attempt to call off the dogs here at all. I say to my hon. friend, go to it, and if you want to keep going here until next Christmas go ahead. As far as I am concerned I would like the minister or someone from his department to give us satisfactory answers to these questions. Go into detail on them. The hon. member for Lethbridge started out on a very important line of questioning about inflation and the integrity of the dollar. If the people of this country, who are labouring under the highest costs in history, take a look at the kind of answers that have come from the government side, the only conclusion they can reach is that nobody here gives a damn whether or not they have to go on paying these high prices.
Watch your language.

I think I have the right to punctuate my remarks a little; and inasmuch as "dam" means to stop, I guess I can use that word. I am taking this position with respect to the assertion made a moment ago by the minister. If he and his department will take a few minutes to get right down to the questions and give us sensible and suitable answers, their estimates will not be held up at all. That is all I am going to say.

I thank the minister most sincerely for putting on record indelibly a statement to the effect that I have done my best in the time at my disposal. I have worked very hard. It does not mean very much to people who have not enough sense to appreciate it, and there are plenty of such people. The important fact is that these questions simply have to be answered.
Who is the judge?

I am the judge. If you can
defend yourself get up and do so; don't yap like a lot of silly pups. Get up and say something.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I would ask the hon. member to address the Chair.
4408

Supply-Finance

Thank you, sir. Of course the chairman will understand that I was not addressing him when I spoke as I did a moment ago. I was asking this question. I asked the parliamentary assistant whether or not one of those $26 million that were created by the finance department of Canada in 1916 and 1917, and spent into circulation, was sound. It is a simple matter to answer that, if he knows how to answer it. If he says it was unsound he knows I shall ask him to prove it, and that he cannot do.
Why ask him then?

Just to show him up. That is what he is here for, is it not? Why do you ask questions of any government minister? To find out whether he knows his business. Is that not right? You ask questions to ascertain whether he knows his business, and that is exactly what I am doing here. We want to know whether or not he knows his business.
He knows his ibusiness.

He should be able to prove it then, and he has not done it thus far. He has not shown he knows anything about it. He does not know anything about sound money, and does not dare even try to define it. He does not know anything about this inflation. He would pretend it is the result of too many dollars chasing too few goods, but we have proved by point after point, what he cannot disprove, that it is a direct result of the profiteering which has forced up the cost of producing and thus of living.
I ask the minister whether one of these $26 million was sound. He knows it was sound. He does not dare say it was sound, however, because if he does he will get into trouble with St. James street and the press all over the country. He does not dare say it was sound, because the very minute he says it was sound he knows that I shall ask him why he does not create a few of suoh dollars now and put them into circulation.. He may say that it would cause inflation. I have already proven, what he cannot possibly disprove, that the so-called inflation is not inflation at all but is the result of the manipulation of prices upward and that there are plenty of goods. I am going to ask the minister once more-he says he has answered the question but he has not answered one of my questions in a straightforward manner -I am going to ask the minister to tell the committee, if he dare, whether or not one of those $26 million which were created and spent into circulation under the Finance Act of 1914 was sound. Such dollars could be created and spent now.
[The Chairman.]
Would you mind repeating that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the time to which my hon. friend refers I was in France, but I think the dollars were probably sound.

I believe the dollars were sound, too. I believe those dollars were sound, and I believe similar dollars issued today and spent into circulation would be sound. I shall defy the minister and all his associates to prove that one of them would not be sound today.
That is the way to talk.
I have issued that defiance several times, and I issue it right now in the presence of plenty of witnesses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It sounds like the marriage ceremony.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There will be a divorce on Friday night.

This morning I spent some time of the house, and I apologize if I have offended any hon. members, showing that the Bradbury which was the war currency that Britain created through her treasury by means of a treasury bill was sound. It was a one pound note. I showed that 354 million of those one-pound notes were printed and circulated in Britain during world war I and up to 1920. I adduced evidence from William A. Shaw's book "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges", and his excellent book "The Theory and Principles of Central Banking" to show that those pound notes were sound.
Go into that a little deeper.
Yes, I shall be glad to do that. They were sound. I do not believe the hon. member was here-
I was here, but I did not quite understand it.

If the hon. member will take Hansard tomorrow and read the speech I made about the Bradbury's, then go to the library and get this book "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges" which tells about the Bradbury's; if he will get the book on "The Theory and Principles of Central Banking", which was written by the same man in 1930, read the quotations I gave and read the books, he will find beyond any shadow of doubt that William A. Shaw considered that money absolutely sound.
Would you mind analysing it?
I shall gladly do that. I do not want to burden anyone, because I went to the trouble of analysing it this morning.
I am interested.

I shall quote something
in addition that William A. Shaw said. Here is a quotation from page 66 of "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges":
The issue of currency is not the affair of a bank. It is the affair of the state, and now that we have established that principle, if we go back on it and sacrifice it we may go still further and sacrifice the automatic principle which is enshrined in the treasury note, and the discovery of which is the greatest achievement of modern economic practice.
Let me analyse that for a minute or two. The hon. member, who has asked me that question so conscientiously, realizes that in this nation today the state does not issue any of the money. The money is issued by the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of Canada, no matter whether or not the government owns it, is a bank. Consequently, the principle which William A. Shaw lays down is violated with the issuance of every dollar that is issued in the Dominion of Canada. Now, that is rather important, is it not? The $26 million in Canada and the treasury notes in Britain that were issued and spent during world war I were issued without any debt. The government did not borrow them; it created them and issued them just the same as the Bank of Canada could create and lend money or issue it.
Here is another quotation from page 67 of the same book.
Eleven o'clock.

It reads:
This theory of money rests upon one basic principle-viz., that goods purchase goods. In this axiom the word "goods" is used for brevity's sake as comprehending all economic goods or services, which as possessing economic value, possess thereby exchange value.
Let me point this out, Mr. Chairman. As I have said time and again from April 19 onward when I started this campaign, the
Supply-Finance
basis of money ought to be goods. This statement about too many dollars chasing too few goods or too few dollars chasing too many goods indicates quite clearly that the real purchasing power in a community is goods and services. This author clearly lays down that principle.

Eleven o'clock.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall take up three resolutions, two in the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, one concerning old age assistance and the other concerning allowances for blind persons. In the past everyone favoured the principle of these resolutions, and I think we should have a short debate because the bills will come up on Saturday. Then, we shall take up the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister concerning the Federal District Commission Act, 1927. We shall then go into supply, and take up the estimates of national health and welfare, public works and the secretary of state. If the committee on veterans affairs complete their work by tomorrow and report the bills they have before them, on Friday we intend to take up the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs and all the bills relating to veterans.
May I ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) whether the three resolutions which he named will be taken up in that order?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
